title: Switzerland - Japanese GreenTech company GSA opens a battery recycling lab in Biel/Bienne - Batteries News
content:
Switzerland – Japanese GreenTech company GSA opens a battery recycling lab in Biel/Bienne
Japanese GreenTech company Green Science Alliance (GSA) has opened a laboratory at Switzerland Innovation Park Biel/Bienne, in the canton of Bern. The lab will develop a technology that regenerates valuable materials from used lithium-ion batteries.
Green Science Alliance (GSA)
, a Japanese chemical and GreenTech company, has opened a laboratory dedicated to next-generation battery recycling at Switzerland Innovation Park Biel/Bienne (SIPBB). Inaugurated on 19 October 2026, the lab operates in partnership with the Swiss Battery Technology Center (SBTC). GSA develops advanced materials for a more sustainable society, from biomass-based alternatives to petroleum-derived products to rechargeable batteries, fuel cells and solar cells.
Regenerating cathode materials directly
Mechanically processing used lithium-ion batteries produces a dark powder called black mass, which contains valuable electrode materials. Conventional recycling dissolves it with acids or bases to recover individual metals, which then need several more processing steps before reuse. GSA’s approach is to directly regenerate the cathode active materials so that they can go back into new batteries, without fully breaking them down into elements. This could cut recycling steps and resource use.
Early results show that batteries made with regenerated cathode materials reached over 90% of the initial capacity of comparable batteries using commercial materials. The technology is being developed for both NMC (nickel-manganese-cobalt) and LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries.
A partnership with SBTC
SBTC is one of the four applied research centers of SIPBB. It provides scientific expertise, infrastructure and lab space, and the joint work covers assessing regenerated materials, making electrodes and cells, testing performance, and evaluating industrial potential and scalability. The partnership is supported by an
Innosuisse
Innovation Cheque, described as a first step toward joint research.
A base for European expansion
GSA chose Biel/Bienne as its base for expanding in Europe, and plans further collaborative R&D. It aims to commercialize the technology in Europe with the help of the SIPBB network of industrial partners, start-ups and research institutions across the battery value chain. If scaled up, the method could reduce the resources needed for recycling, lessen reliance on newly mined raw materials and support more resilient European battery supply chains.

title: GM to close Detroit battery assembly plant, but not for reasons you might think - Batteries News
content:
GM to close Detroit battery assembly plant, but not for reasons you might think
GM is closing a battery-assembly plant south of Detroit, a spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch.
The Brownstown Battery Assembly Plant assembled battery packs for Cadillac’s flagship EV, the Celestiq, and both electric drive units (the motors that power the car) and battery packs for the Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray, a plug-in hybrid version of its famous sports car. Automotive News first reported the closure.
The closure is not related to GM’s electric vehicle strategy, the spokesperson said. Instead, GM leased the site, and the lease was nearing its end.
The employees and work at Brownstown will be moved to other GM facilities, though the company would not confirm which ones.
Like many automakers, GM’s electrification strategy was thrown a curveball after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the sweeping federal law signed last year, repealed incentives to produce and sell EVs.
Since then, the company has pared back its public comments on EVs, though it hasn’t given up on full electrification.
GM continues to produce a range of EVs, including the Chevrolet Silverado EV and the limited-time-only Chevrolet Bolt. It also continues researching new battery chemistries, including lithium-manganese-rich and sodium-ion, and it’s rolling out a new $900 million facility to speed commercialization.

title: CATL Unveils Dual-Electric Range Extension Battery to Accelerate Electric Heavy-Duty Truck Adoption - Batteries News
content:
CATL Unveils Dual-Electric Range Extension Battery to Accelerate Electric Heavy-Duty Truck Adoption
BEIJING, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — CATL today unveiled the innovative dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation.
Competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilization, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics.
To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with QIJI’s strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification.
A Dual-Electric Approach to Range Extension
CATL’s dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems.
The main battery uses QIJI’s standardized chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions.
Dual-System Power Redundancy
In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery’s depth of discharge (DOD) from approximately 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold, CATL’s seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply.
“1+X” Architecture and Independent Upgrades
The system uses a “1+X” architecture. One standardized main battery maintains compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customized for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power.
The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements.
Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management
The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly.
This architecture combines the benefits of standardization with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications.
QIJI Builds a Shared Battery Swapping Ecosystem
QIJI complements these improvements with a three-pillar strategy of
standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem
. It seeks to speed heavy-duty truck electrification with a value-chain ecosystem co-created by all stakeholders, where benefits are shared collectively.
Standardization Supports Wider Adoption
To accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions, QIJI has introduced the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized battery-swapping blocks alongside the existing 75# block.
The system enables battery swaps in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate, helping fleets minimize downtime and maintain operational efficiency.
QIJI has also pioneered a battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model in which customers pay for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged. This allows customers to retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking, reducing per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%. Flexible battery leasing options allow customers to tailor rental periods to their needs, from second-hand vehicle transitions to seasonal demand. This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs.
New Infrastructure Improves Resource Efficiency
QIJI aims to make better use of four critical resources in long-haul freight: time, land, payload capacity and grid electricity. Rapid battery swapping reduces waiting times, while efficient station layouts serve more vehicles within the same footprint. Battery capacity is matched to transport needs, and centralized, coordinated charging makes better use of grid electricity. These measures aim to improve both resource efficiency and operational returns.
CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations nationwide in collaboration with its partners.
A Commercial Ecosystem Supports the Full Vehicle Lifecycle
QIJI connects truck manufacturers, financial institutions, insurers, channel partners and aftermarket service providers across the vehicle lifecycle, from purchase and operation to maintenance and resale, working together to build a comprehensive ecosystem of integrated products and services.
QIJI has introduced two partnership models:
Battery Asset Service Partners
Energy Replenishment Service Partners
. These models allow partners to participate in battery asset services and energy replenishment, extending their role beyond one-off vehicle sales to ongoing operations.
Through this integrated ecosystem, QIJI aims to turn the costs of the low-carbon transition into new growth opportunities, enabling stakeholders across the value chain to share the benefits of the new-energy era.
Jesse Yang,
CEO of QIJI Energy, said:
The combination of the dual-electric range extension battery and QIJI battery swapping offers the best solution for electrifying heavy-duty trucks,
New Batteries and Industry Partnerships
The initiative has also gained commercial traction, with agreements signed for 13,000 units at the event.
Aside from the dual-electric solution, CATL also introduced a new lineup of heavy-duty truck batteries tailored to different vehicle configurations and operating requirements at the event. The lineup includes rear-mounted ultra-light and ultra-thin batteries for weight- and space-sensitive applications, as well as chassis-mounted solutions for short-haul and long-haul operations.

title: Volkswagen to recall over 70,000 EVs worldwide due to faulty batteries - Batteries News
content:
Volkswagen to recall over 70,000 EVs worldwide due to faulty batteries
Volkswagen has issued a recall for nearly 72,700 electric vehicles due to faulty batteries, according to data from the German Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) published on Tuesday.
Some 10,000 vehicles, largely from Volkswagen’s ID line, are affected in Germany alone.
It became known last week that Volkswagen was preparing a recall, after internal quality checks found that individual high-voltage battery cells in certain ID family vehicles do not meet quality requirements. The cause is production defects at suppliers, affecting a limited production period, according to Volkswagen.
The company
said last week,
In rare cases, this can lead to increased thermal stress on these batteries; in extreme cases, a fire could break out
Models affected include the ID.3, ID.4, ID.7 and ID.Buzz from certain production periods between 2022 and 2025, as well as the Cupra Born built by Spanish subsidiary Cupra between 2022 and 2024.
Affected customers will receive a letter, the company said.
As an immediate measure, Volkswagen is limiting charging of the affected vehicles to a maximum of 80% for safety reasons, until the car is checked by a workshop. The affected battery modules might not necessarily have to be replaced, as a software update might be enough, according to Volkswagen.
This is not the company’s first recall this year over battery problems: In March, Volkswagen and Cupra had already called in more than 90,000 cars worldwide for the same reason – 28,000 of them in Germany.
At the end of September, the carmaker also called in just over 5 million cars worldwide to workshops over a corrosion-prone screw on the steering system.

title: Fraunhofer ISE Successfully Tests High-Energy Battery Cells with Silicon-Rich Anodes Over 1,000 Cycles - Batteries News
content:
Fraunhofer ISE Successfully Tests High-Energy Battery Cells with Silicon-Rich Anodes Over 1,000 Cycles
Silicon-rich lithium-ion batteries promise high energy densities for applications in electric mobility, aerospace, and stationary energy storage. However, their industrial application has so far been limited primarily by their limited cycle life. In the project “StrOboBatt,” researchers at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE succeeded in operating in-house-manufactured 25-Ah pouch cells with silicon-rich anodes for more than 1,000 full cycles. The full cells subsequently retained over 83 percent of their original capacity, with a gravimetric energy density of 280 Wh/kg in a non-optimized research cell format. This marks an important step toward the application of silicon-rich anodes in high-energy batteries.
Dr. Lukas Dold,
team leader for battery materials technology and scaling at Fraunhofer ISE, explains,
Cycle life is one of the key hurdles to the widespread industrial use of silicon-rich anodes.
”More than 1,000 cycles with a capacity retention of at least 80 percent is considered an important performance target here. With our pouch cells, we were able to achieve this goal while also demonstrating a gravimetric energy density of 280 Wh/kg at the cell level in the PrecISE research cell format designed by Fraunhofer ISE. In an industrially optimized pouch cell format, a gravimetric energy density of approximately 330 Wh/kg is expected.”
Industrial-scale pouch cells with silicon-rich anodes
In the “StrOboBatt—Structure- and Surface-Optimized Silicon Anodes and High-Energy Cathodes for High-Energy-Density Lithium-Ion Batteries” project, the team fabricated multilayer full cells (40 layers) with a capacity of 25 Ah. Commercially available electrode foils were used, featuring a silicon-carbon/graphite anode and a nickel-rich nickel-manganese-cobalt oxide cathode. Compared to graphite, which is currently used as an anode material, silicon has a theoretical specific capacity that is ten times higher. When used in structurally optimized silicon-carbon composites, it can reduce global dependence on graphite as a raw material. This would allow value creation—particularly in raw material extraction—to be shifted toward the EU. In the test cells, the silicon-carbon composite accounted for 51 percent of the anode active material. The anodes achieve a specific capacity of more than 1,000 mAh/g and a areal specific capacity of more than 5 mAh/cm².
The multilayer pouch cells were manufactured on a semi-automatic production line in the cleanroom of the Center for Electrical Energy Storage at Fraunhofer ISE. They thus combine high electrode capacities with an industry-standard cell format and serve as reference cells in the project for evaluating new materials, cell designs, and operating conditions.
In addition to cycle life, the researchers investigated the effect of mechanical pressure on the pouch cells during operation. To do this, the cells were charged and discharged (1 C operation) within one hour at two different axial contact pressures (300 and 1,000 kPa, respectively). External axial pressure applied to the cell results, among other things, in improved interfacial resistance and reduces the risk of the electrode materials detaching from one another and from the substrate, which is particularly relevant for silicon-containing anodes. Through regular check-up cycles at lower current rates, the influence of pressure on cycle stability could be evaluated.
Marc Kissling,
group leader for battery cell production and technology evaluation at Fraunhofer ISE, explains,
Axial pressure has a significant impact on the long-term behavior of the cells.
”At a contact pressure of 1,000 kPa, our cells still retain over 83 percent of their original capacity even after more than 1,000 full cycles. At a lower contact pressure of 300 kPa, a significantly greater decline in usable capacity over time is observed, particularly during 1C operation. Mechanical cell pressure is therefore an important parameter for the stable operation of silicon-rich pouch cells.”
At the same time, the studies reveal a growing discrepancy between the residual capacity determined at a low discharge rate and the capacity available during regular 1C operation. This underscores that, when evaluating silicon-rich cells, their performance under real-world operating conditions must be taken into account in addition to pure capacity retention.
At Fraunhofer ISE, new battery materials can be investigated along the entire process chain—from electrode fabrication to the electrochemical characterization of large-format pouch cells. The existing infrastructure includes, among other things, batch mixing, roll-to-roll coating, pouch cell assembly, as well as cell formation and electrochemical characterization.
Marc Kissling
Since we can map the entire process chain in-house—from mixing the electrode materials to electrochemical characterization—new materials and cell concepts can be validated under industry-standard conditions throughout the entire manufacturing process,

title: Hanwha Power Receives ABS Approval in Principle for 1,700 TEU Battery Powered Containership Design - Batteries News
content:
Hanwha Power Receives ABS Approval in Principle for 1,700 TEU Battery Powered Containership Design
Fully electric propulsion design featuring approximately 151 MWh of energy storage strengthens capabilities in zero-carbon maritime transport
Integrated solution combines electric propulsion, and containerized battery energy storage systems
Expanded eco-friendly marine propulsion portfolio lays the groundwork for
entry into the next-generation zero-carbon vessel market
SEOUL, South Korea, Oct. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Hanwha Power announced that it had received Approval in Principle (AiP) from the American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) for its design of a 1,700 TEU battery-powered containership.
The certificate presentation ceremony took place on October 22, local time, at the MHE (Maritime Hybrid, Electric & Hydrogen Fuel Cells) Conference & Exhibition 2026 in Bergen, Norway. Jong-kyu Hwang, Vice President, Technology Solutions at Hanwha Power, attended the ceremony alongside senior representatives from ABS. The event runs from October 21 to 23 at the Scandic Hotel Bergen City.
The newly approved design concept features a fully electric container vessel powered by a large-scale 151 MWh Energy Storage System (ESS). Electrical energy stored in containerized battery units serves as the vessel’s primary propulsion source, enabling operation without direct carbon emissions through the use of port charging infrastructure.
The use of containerized batteries, which can be handled and stowed like standard cargo containers, enhances space efficiency, maximizes cargo capacity, and optimizes overall vessel performance. This approach also supports flexible battery replacement and scalable operation, offering a practical pathway for the decarbonization of short-sea and regional container transport.
The AiP strengthens Hanwha Power’s capabilities in fully electric vessel design using large-scale battery energy storage and expands its portfolio of marine propulsion solutions. The company plans to build on this achievement to pursue opportunities in the next-generation zero-carbon maritime transport market.
Alongside the approval, Hanwha Power has also completed the basic design of a 1,000 TEU battery-powered container vessel. Building on its expertise in vessel design across multiple ship classes, the company aims to develop a comprehensive lineup of electric-propulsion vessels tailored to a wide range of operating conditions and customer needs.
Jong-kyu Hwang,
Vice President, Technology Solutions at Hanwha Power, said:
This AiP from ABS marks an important step in extending Hanwha Power’s marine technology capabilities to fully electric vessels powered by large-scale battery systems,
“We will address the needs of the next-generation zero-carbon maritime transport market with integrated solutions that combine electric propulsion and containerized battery system technologies.”

title: Camel Group at the 140th Canton Fair - LEV Battery Products Expand Its Multi- Technology Portfolio for Global Mobility - Batteries News
content:
Camel Group at the 140th Canton Fair – LEV Battery Products Expand Its Multi- Technology Portfolio for Global Mobility
WUHAN, China, Oct. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — On October 15, 2026, the 140th China Import and Export Fair (Canton Fair) opened in Guangzhou. Phase 1 is held under the theme “Advanced Manufacturing.” Camel Group is showcasing SLI, EFB and AGM automotive low-voltage lead-acid batteries, low-voltage lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries, as well as battery products for light electric vehicles (LEVs). The lineup covers vehicle starting, auxiliary power, engine-off power for parked vehicles, and low-speed mobility applications.
Among this year’s additions are LEV battery products for electric two- and three-wheelers, low-speed four-wheelers and golf carts, addressing different requirements for range, payload, cycle life and total cost of ownership.
Camel’s lithium-ion LEV batteries are built on 64V and 76.8V platforms, with capacities from 20Ah to 206Ah. Featuring lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells and an intelligent battery management system (BMS), the products support applications including daily commuting, last-mile delivery, cargo transport, and construction and utility vehicles.
Building on more than four decades of lead-acid expertise, Camel has developed lead-acid batteries for LEVs across 6V, 8V and 12V platforms, with capacities from 13.3Ah to 150Ah. They deliver reliable performance and deep-cycle life across different duty cycles and range requirements.
For automotive low-voltage applications, Camel is displaying SLI, EFB and AGM lead-acid batteries alongside low-voltage lithium-ion and sodium-ion products. Its lithium-ion portfolio spans 12V to 48V architectures, supporting vehicle starting, auxiliary and backup power, commercial-vehicle parking air-conditioning systems, and 48V electrical systems.
Camel’s 12V sodium-ion battery is now part of a pre-development project with a European automotive manufacturer, with technical development and validation work to follow. title: Hanbat National University Study Shows Cation Disorder Could Improve Lithium-Rich Cathodes - Batteries News
content:
Hanbat National University Study Shows Cation Disorder Could Improve Lithium-Rich Cathodes
Experiments show a disordered structure enhances lithium transport while preventing performance degradation
CHUNGCHEONG PROVINCE, South Korea, Oct. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Lithium-rich cathodes could be key to developing batteries with higher energy densities. However, transition metal ions can drift out of place during operation, blocking lithium transport. In a recent study, researchers from Korea tackled this issue by intentionally introducing disorder in the cathode’s atomic structure. This strategy resulted in improved performance and stability, highlighting a potential new route toward higher-energy batteries for applications like electric vehicles and energy storage.
Lithium-rich cathode materials promise higher energy density for next-generation batteries in electronics and electric vehicles, but they suffer from performance loss when migrating metal ions block lithium pathways. Although scientists traditionally tried to preserve an orderly crystal structure to prevent this issue, a recent study by Professor Kyojin Ku’s team at Hanbat National University, Korea, explored an unconventional approach. Made available online on July 18, 2026, and published in Volume 90 of Energy Storage Materials on August 1, 2026, their research focused on intentionally disrupting the cathode’s atomic structure instead.
The team focused on Li
, a nickel-manganese composition that avoids expensive metals like cobalt. This particular composition normally forms a neatly layered structure, where lithium and transition-metal ions (nickel and manganese) sit in separate planes. To produce the desired disordered form, the researchers used high-energy ball milling with two structurally compatible layered starting materials. This mechanochemical process disrupted the arrangement of the cations, resulting in a crystal structure where lithium and transition-metal ions are distributed more randomly.
Prof. Ku
, remarks:
To our knowledge, this is the first time this type of composition has been made in the disordered form
Detailed theoretical and computational analysis helped explain the observed improvements.
Prof. Ku,
explains:
“Lithium still flows efficiently through a connected network of open pathways, while the transition-metals become effectively locked in place and can no longer block those pathways.”
Overall, the findings point to an innovative and impactful approach for developing higher-energy-density cathodes.
Prof. Ku
, concludes:
We have shown that cation disorder can be used as a deliberate engineering tool to solve a problem that has held back an entire family of high-energy battery materials for years,
“If this principle is developed further, it could help move lithium-rich cathodes closer to real commercial use, paving the way for longer-lasting batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage.”

LG Energy Solution – AI Data Center Power Solutions: From BBUs and UPS Batteries to Grid-Scale BESS
LG Energy Solution showcased a battery portfolio for AI data centers at Data Centre World Asia 2026, spanning server-level BBUs, facility-level UPS batteries and grid-scale BESS.
Through the One LG AI Factory, LG Energy Solution, LG Electronics and LG CNS are combining power, cooling, construction and operational capabilities to address next-generation AI infrastructure needs.
Under the theme “End-to-End AI Factory Infrastructure Partner,” the joint booth addressed infrastructure requirements across the AIDC lifecycle. Within this ecosystem, LG Energy Solution showcased battery solutions for key power infrastructure needs, including Battery Backup Units (BBUs), Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) batteries, and Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS).
Growing AI Workloads Increase Demand for Data Center Power Infrastructure
As AIDCs become larger and computing workloads become more intensive, reliable power infrastructure is increasingly important. Higher compute density requires systems that can support continuous operation and protect servers and critical equipment from even brief interruptions.
Battery-based solutions help meet these needs by providing immediate backup power at the server-rack level and supporting energy management across the facility and grid.
Battery Solutions for Different Power Needs: From Server Racks to the Grid
At the server level, LG Energy Solution showcased its
2170 cylindrical
battery for BBUs. Installed on power racks, BBUs can provide immediate Direct Current (DC) power to IT racks during unexpected power interruptions and help maintain stability. Customer examples and video content illustrated how these capabilities can support power stability and operational efficiency in AIDCs.
For facility-level backup power, LG Energy Solution exhibited the JP5 designed to provide high energy density within a compact footprint. The system delivers 1MW-class power in a 1m² footprint, helping address space constraints for backup power infrastructure.
The JP5 also incorporates a Self-Powered Switched-Mode Power Supply (SMPS), allowing its Battery Management System (BMS) and Battery Protection Unit (BPU) to operate independently without an external power source. Together with
UL9540A certification
, these features are designed to support the safety and reliability of backup power systems in data center environments.
At the grid level, the company presented the JF2 DC Link, an
LFP-based
, long-cell BESS designed to provide large-scale energy storage for power infrastructure supporting AIDCs. The system offers 5.0MWh-class energy capacity in a single 22.1-foot
container, with liquid-cooling thermal management and UL9540A safety certification.
The JF2 DC Link also features LG Energy Solution’s proprietary State-of-Charge (SOC) Calibration Free technology. By maintaining SOC accuracy without separate calibration, the technology supports more efficient management of large-scale energy storage systems.
In addition, LG Energy Solution promoted its JF2 AC Link through a dedicated pop-up banner. The product, targeted primarily at North American utility customers, was highlighted as meeting NVIDIA DSX Ready requirements.
Connecting Power, Cooling, and Construction Through the One LG AI Factory
LG Energy Solution’s presence at
DCWA 2026
extended beyond individual battery products. The joint booth also demonstrated the One LG AI Factory concept, which brings together LG Energy Solution’s battery and power infrastructure technologies, LG Electronics’ cooling solutions, and LG CNS’s expertise in AIDC construction and operations.
Visitors explored how gigawatt-scale AIDCs are constructed and operated through interactive dioramas, video content, and prefabricated modular AI Factory solutions that can shorten construction timelines.
Meeting AI Power Demands
As AI power demands continue to increase, AI infrastructure requires solutions across multiple layers, from server-level backup to facility-level power continuity and grid-scale energy management. The One LG AI Factory offers an integrated approach to meet power, cooling, construction and operations needs as AIDCs become larger and more complex. LG Energy Solution is committed to meeting these requirements through BBUs, UPS batteries and BESS, providing solutions across different levels of AIDC power infrastructure.

title: Avicenne Energy, Li-Bridge Standardize Battery Readiness
content:
Battery Manufacturing
Battery News
Avicenne Energy and Li-Bridge teamed up with industry stakeholders to standardize how battery programs measure technical and manufacturing maturity.
November 6, 2026
5 Min Read
EV battery manufacturing
PhonlamaiPhoto/iStock / Getty Images Plus
At a Glance
Avicenne Energy and Li-Bridge created a framework to standardize TRL and MRL definitions across the battery industry.
The biggest gap: TRL 4-6, where companies struggle to scale from prototypes to automated, repeatable production.
Stellantis already uses the framework to spot gaps between technical readiness and manufacturing maturity.
Battery manufacturers love to talk about Technology Readiness Levels (TRL) and Manufacturing Readiness Levels (MRL). The problem is, they rarely mean the same thing when they do.
One company's "pilot production" is another's "pre-production," and a program that looks mature on paper might be nowhere near scalable. That gap between what a battery technology can do and what a factory can actually produce has quietly become one of the industry's biggest blind spots.
To close it, Avicenne Energy teamed up with Li-Bridge — the public-private alliance working to build a stronger domestic lithium-battery supply chain — along with a group of leading industry stakeholders. Together, they built a standardized
Readiness Assessment Framework
designed to bring order to the messy, inconsistent world of TRL and MRL definitions.
Why readiness got so confusing
TRL and MRL sound similar, but they measure very different things.
tracks how mature the technology itself is — does the chemistry work, does the cell perform, is the concept validated? It typically runs from 0 to 9.
tracks something else entirely: can that technology actually be manufactured, consistently and at scale? It usually runs from 1 to 10.
Related:
Battery Show North America 2026: Technology Highlights From the Show Floor
Here's the simplest way to think about it: TRL asks "does it work?" MRL asks "can we make it, reliably, in the volumes we need?"
A battery program can score well on TRL while its MRL lags far behind. The chemistry might be excellent in the lab, but the manufacturing process hasn't been automated, standardized, or proven at scale yet. That disconnect is exactly where many programs run into trouble — and exactly what makes a shared readiness language so important.
Battery cells for automotive industry on production line. Credit: SweetBunFactory / iStock / Getty Images Plus
The industry pressure behind the problem
A few forces are converging to make this issue harder to ignore. EV and energy storage demand keeps pushing automakers to industrialize new battery technologies faster than ever, while federal agencies are increasingly weaving MRL terminology into grants and partnerships. At the same time, startups, OEMs, and suppliers all define "readiness" differently, making cross-industry benchmarking nearly impossible — and "pilot production" has become a catch-all term that can mean wildly different things depending on who's using it.
Without a common framework, companies risk overestimating how close a program really is to commercial scale — a costly mistake when capital, timelines, and partnerships are on the line.
What the framework actually found
The project zeroed in on the critical TRL 4-6 / MRL 3-5 window — the stage where a battery program moves from early technical validation toward manufacturable, repeatable, increasingly automated production. This is where most of the industry's confusion (and risk) lives.
Related:
QuantumScape Plans 100-MWh Line to Chase AI Data-Center & Defense Markets
Working with Li-Bridge and industry input, the team built volume criteria tied to each TRL and MRL stage, mapping out exactly what "readiness" should look like at each point. A few key findings stood out:
TRL 1-3 — R&D pilot lines are everywhere.
The U.S. has plenty of facilities supporting early-stage material and cell development. They could use tighter SOPs and more standardization, but capacity isn't the issue here.
TRL 4-6 — This is the real gap.
Producing thousands of cells using standard, automated techniques is where the U.S. market falls short. This is the bridge between "it works in the lab" and "we can actually scale it" — and right now, there's a serious shortage of capacity at this stage.
TRL 7-9 — Thin, but growing.
Higher-volume pre-production capability is still limited, though private companies are increasingly stepping in to meet customer demand.
For OEMs and large manufacturers, levels beyond TRL 6 are often managed through internal systems like Stage-Gate, PSDP, or MPRQ — meaning the framework's biggest value shows up earlier in the journey, right when programs are deciding whether they're truly ready to scale.
Related:
Inside the 2026 Battery Awards, Where Innovation Took Center Stage
Framework-driven diagnostic analysis. Credit: Avicenne Energy
Choosing a path forward
Using the standardized framework creates a consistent, disciplined way to evaluate readiness across technologies, projects, and organizations. It enables clearer benchmarking, improves alignment around what “ready” actually means, and helps identify gaps earlier in the development process, when they are typically less costly and easier to address. The result is better-informed decision-making and a more structured path toward commercialization and scale.
Avicenne Energy's full case study breaks down the complete comparison between these approaches, along with the five-phase implementation roadmap used to roll the framework out.
Read the full case study here
The results so far
Stellantis is among the companies already putting the framework to work after making some adjustments to the structure to better fit its industrialization processes. The impact has been tangible: greater discipline and rigor in battery program reviews, a clearer read on where programs truly stand, and — perhaps most valuable — early visibility into the gap between what the technology can do and what the factory can actually produce.
That visibility has helped teams avoid overstating readiness and make more informed calls about when to scale.
The bigger lesson
Inconsistent definitions aren't just a semantics problem — they're a business risk. When teams, partners, and investors don't share the same readiness language, collaboration breaks down and scale-up decisions get riskier.
A common framework fixes that. It's not just useful for automakers — cell manufacturers, materials suppliers, pack and component makers, energy storage system builders, pilot line operators, equipment suppliers, and investors all face the same readiness ambiguity. Anyone trying to move a promising battery technology from the lab to the production line stands to benefit from a framework that finally draws a clear line between "it works" and "we can build it."

title: Sodium-Ion Batteries Gain Ground in Australia’s Energy Market
content:
Materials
Battery Applications
Industry Outlook
Interviews
Sodium-ion batteries are challenging LFP in Australia, with growing momentum in household storage, grid systems, safety, commercialization and future scale.
November 6, 2026
4 Min Read
Sodium-ion (Na-ion) batteries are an alternative to lithium-ion batteries.
2265191331/iStock / Getty Images Plus
Neeraj Sharma,
Director at the Australian Battery Society & Professor of Chemistry at
UNSW Sydney
, recently gave a free public talk on sodium-ion batteries at
ScienceKind
as part of its new Tuesday series, “From Atoms to Grids”. Sharma brought a true lab-bench perspective to a topic attracting growing attention across the energy industry. Following the talk,
Battery Technology
interviewed him, extending the discussion beyond the presentation to explore why sodium-ion batteries matter now and what may come next.
How does sodium-ion compare with LFP today, and where do you see its strongest advantage?
Neeraj Sharma, Director at the Australian Battery Society & Professor of Chemistry at UNSW Sydney:
Generally speaking,
sodium-ion batteries
with the current generation of components (cathodes and anodes) are comparable to LFP. They are comparable in terms of energy density and, depending on the cathode/anode choice, can be cheaper, but this does depend on the price of lithium.
Related:
ExxonMobil on Building a Competitive & Resilient North American Graphite Supply Chain
They can be discharged to 0 V and so can be safer to transport than the LFP counterparts. In my opinion, one of the key aspects for sodium-ion battery technology is to validate the lifetime of the cells and to validate this under different load conditions and under different external conditions (e.g., temperatures, etc.).
What developments are you seeing in Australia that suggest sodium-ion is gaining real momentum?
As I said in the interview with ScienceKind, sodium-ion batteries have an opportunity to displace LFP systems in household storage and grid-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS). That is where the opportunity lies, and we are seeing companies trying to bring these systems to market. The smaller household units are easier to commercialize, as the larger BESS tend to go for safer, tried and tested technology. We did have situations earlier in the year where guidelines and such were for lithium-ion battery systems, e.g., rebate and certification schemes, which required modification to include sodium-ion battery systems.
Battery energy storage system with solar and turbine farms. Courtesy of PhonlamaiPhoto/ iStock / Getty Images Plus.
How is Australia contributing to the progress of sodium-ion batteries right now?
We have commercial entities that are bringing sodium-ion battery systems to Australia for household-scale storage and specialised applications. There is interest in local firms adapting to this technology as well and potentially producing modules based on sodium-ion cells in-country. We have other firms investigating the viability of producing cells in Australia for specialised applications. This opens up new opportunities for growth and development.
Related:
SPE Names Three Finalists for EV Innovation Award
In terms of research and development, there are number of active research groups working electrode, electrolyte and separator materials. Research ranges from materials discovery to electrode formulations to completely new concepts in device construction. Researchers are looking at a variety of electrolytes, including traditional carbonates to ionic liquids and solid-state. Research is also engaging in understanding recycling and the impact sodium-ion batteries will have on recycling streams and value. A number of research projects are being licensed and spun out of research institutes.
Which applications do you see as the best near-term fit for sodium-ion batteries, grid storage, EVs or something else, and why?
As mentioned above, household and grid-scale storage is probably the best utilization for sodium-ion batteries. Essentially, here mass/weight and size/shape is not as much of an issue as say portable and mobility applications. Research and development is working on factors such as depth of cycling, cycling rates, cycling conditions and lifetime to understand how batteries behave under different conditions. As these discoveries and know-how become more established, uptake may increase.
Looking ahead over the next five years, what should the industry be watching most closely to judge whether sodium-ion will truly scale?
Firstly, not all lithium-ion batteries are the same; there are NMC, NCA, LFP, and LTO-based lithium-ion batteries. A similar case is true for sodium-ion systems. The lithium-ion and sodium-ion systems are evolving as well; we are seeing Si-graphite in the anode for lithium-ion batteries and different chemistries appearing for electrode components in sodium-ion systems. There will be a mix of battery chemistries for different applications, much like NMC, NCA, and LiCoO2 cathodes in lithium-ion batteries dominate the portable electronics market and LFP tends to dominate the lithium-ion battery household/grid-scale storage markets. We are likely to see a similar range of chemistries in the sodium-ion battery space for different applications.
Related:

Walmart has agreed a US$6bn deal with Symbotic to expand the installation of Symbotic's solutions across its regional distribution network in North America. Credit: Symbotic
Walmart EVP US Supply Chain Rob Montgomery explains why Walmart is investing US$6bn to expand Symbotic automation across 42 regional distribution centres
Global retail giant Walmart has expanded its strategic partnership with warehouse automation leader Symbotic in a multi-year agreement valued at approximately US$6bn. The initiative aims to deploy advanced artificial intelligence and robotics across a further 25 regional distribution centres in North America to radically optimise upstream inventory management.
The agreement covers the installation of Symbotic's BreakPack each-picking system alongside SymMicro micro-fulfilment solution for ecommerce. Powered by proprietary AI algorithms, these digital logistics solutions orchestrate the movement of millions of cases daily.
"Our work with Symbotic over the years, including this expanded agreement, helps us improve service, grow capacity, simplify work for our associates and lower costs," comments Rob Montgomery, Executive Vice President for Walmart US Supply Chain Operations.
Rob Montgomery, EVP Supply Chain at Walmart
Under the terms of the agreement, Walmart is also entering into a development agreement, under which Walmart will commit US$125m to fund the research and development of next-generation racking and picking technologies as well as process flow and inventory management capabilities.
"Our partnership with Walmart started with a single product over a decade ago, and now we offer a full end-to-end solution to help power Walmart's growth across its supply chain for years to come," Rick Cohen, Chairman and CEO of Symbotic comments.
Symbotic has partnered with Walmart to automate all 42 of its general-merchandise distribution centres by around 2030. The new agreement extends the scope of previous agreements, which covered the deployment of SymmMicro to hundreds of micro-fulfilment centres attached to Walmart stores in North America.
Symbotic offers flexible, ultra-high density warehouse automation solutions. Credit: Symbotic
Longstanding relationship

relationship
between Symbotic and Walmart. Walmart has been
collaborating
with Symbotic since 2017. Walmart has been the main client for Symbotic's solutions for a number of years: under the terms of the latest agreement, Symbotic has conceded that Walmart can appoint two non-voting board observers in years where it accounts for more than 50% of Symbotic's revenue.
In January 2025, Walmart divested its Advanced Systems and Robotics business to Symbotic and concurrently agreed to commission Symbotic to develop, build and deploy a micro-fulfilment solution, SymmMicro, using Symbotic’s AI-enabled robotics platform. At the time of the agreement, Walmart agreed to deploy the delivery of its solution to micro-fulfilment centres attached to 400 stores in North America. The systems are intended to accelerate the fulfilment of ecommerce orders at the APDs, lowering the speed to 12 minutes.

Deployment of SymMicro micro-fulfilment systems to support faster ecommerce order preparation.
Expansion of high-density storage capacity to significantly improve upstream inventory management algorithms.
Use of proprietary AI software to perfectly orchestrate high-volume daily case movements.

title: GXO’s Strategic Logistics Hub: Growth Across Asia Pacific
content:
GXO’s Strategic Logistics Hub: Growth Across Asia Pacific
Prioritise Us

GXO is expanding operations with a new APAC hub. Credit: GXO
Scott Copeland, Managing Director, Asia Pacific at GXO explains how the new hub will aid with operational growth and meeting demand
GXO is growing its footprint, gaining a new strategic hub in Malaysia. The APAC region is undergoing rapid transformation in the logistics sector, driven by the adoption of automation, growing consumption and changing supply chains.
Global disruption has demonstrated that logistics needs to change, which has driven organisations across APAC to rethink how networks operate.
Alongside this, organisations are growing their global footprint, understanding that a network needs to be global in order to withstand volatility.
Supply chain resilience
GXO Logistics, the largest pure-play contract logistics provider, has announced the opening of a new logistics hub in Medini, Malaysia. Demonstrative of its commitment to the fast-growing region, GXO is working strategically to grow its standing in the area.
In 2024, APAC led the global logistics market, driven by stronger trade activity and the accelerated adoption of advanced logistics technologies.
This has continued to shift in recent years, driven by various geopolitical disruptions and a growing understanding of the need for diversification. Companies around the world are turning away from a single production area, as well as working hard to break into new markets.
To avoid supply chain risks that are limited to one area, organisations are diversifying production around the world. Alongside this, they are recognising the importance of storing goods closer to the customer.
Businesses are reducing risk by diversifying across Southeast Asia and India, alongside maintaining operational continuity
amid volatility and controlling costs
more effectively.
Asia Pacific continues to be one of the most dynamic growth markets for GXO.
Michael Jacobs, Chief Executive Officer of the Americas and Asia Pacific at GXO
Strategic positioning
Alongside the risk-reduction behind diversification in logistics, it is also a crucial step in ensuring customer satisfaction. The rise of social commerce is increasing the need for
cross-border trade
, with consumers finding more products through social media.
Due to the global reach of these platforms, trade is becoming more global. As a result, there is a core need for a strong, global logistics network.
GXO’s new hub is located in the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (SEZ), which has all the benefits of a Free Trade Zone (FTZ), as well as access to one of the region;s most strategically positioned logistics corridors.
It has close connectivity to major manufacturing centres, airports and ports, meaning that companies can optimise their inventory positioning. This results in more resilient supply chains and reduced operating costs.
“Asia Pacific continues to be one of the most dynamic growth markets for GXO,” explains Michael Jacobs, Chief Executive Officer of the Americas and Asia Pacific at GXO.
Michael Jacobs, Chief Executive Officer of the Americas and Asia Pacific at GXO
“The opening of our Medini facility reflects our commitment to bringing world-class logistics solutions to high-growth markets. From its strategic location within the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone, the site will offer customers greater flexibility, resilience and speed while connecting them with some of the region’s most important manufacturing, technology and trade hubs.”
At a glance
GXO has more than 1,000 warehouse locations
The company has operations in 27 countries
More than 200 million square feet of warehouse space makes up GXO’s operations
30% of Fortune 100 companies are in its customer base
GXO has more than 150K team members
Improving customer service
The new facility is specifically designed to support customers across advanced industrial sectors and technology. It is currently the regional hub for major global supplier or semiconductor manufacturing equipment, meaning the facility is well-designed for critical technology.
GXO is also exploring growth within the site, including capabilities for emerging warehouse technologies. An aim for this is to drive collaboration between GXO and its customers, as well as increased visibility across the supply chain.
“As technology and advanced manufacturing continue to expand in Asia Pacific, companies are increasingly looking for ways to position inventory closer to regional demand,” said Scott Copeland, Managing Director, Asia Pacific at GXO.
Scott Copeland, Managing Director, Asia Pacific at GXO
“With access to Singapore and southern Malaysia’s key ports and manufacturing hubs, our new Medini site gives customers a strategic base to scale efficiently and serve both regional and global markets.”
Key partners
GXO Logistics is the world's largest pure-play contract logistics provider, spun off from XPO Logistics in 2021. Headquartered in Connecticut, GXO operates warehouses and distribution centers globally, serving sectors including e-commerce, retail, and technology. The company specializes in automated warehousing solutions, reverse logistics, and supply chain optimization. With over 200 million square feet of warehouse space across 970+ locations, GXO employs approximately 130,000 people worldwide, delivering innovative logistics technology and services.
Agility Robotics
Agility Robotics, founded in 2015 in Oregon, develops advanced bipedal robots for logistics and industry. Their flagship product, Digit, is a human-sized robot designed to navigate human environments and handle packages in warehouses. Digit features human-like mobility, can lift 35 pounds, and works alongside human employees. The company opened RoboFab, their manufacturing facility, in 2023, capable of producing 10,000+ units annually, targeting logistics companies and e-commerce fulfillment operations.
Columbia Sportswear
Columbia Sportswear Company, founded in Portland, Oregon in 1938, is a global outdoor apparel and footwear leader. The family-controlled company owns brands including Columbia, Mountain Hardwear, SOREL, and prAna. Known for innovative technologies like Omni-Heat thermal reflective and OutDry waterproofing, Columbia generates over $3 billion in annual revenue. Operating in 90+ countries with 400+ retail stores, the company designs performance gear for hiking, skiing, fishing, and everyday outdoor activities.

title: Yamaha’s new electric scooter takes aim at Europe’s 125cc commuters
content:
Electric Motorcycles
electric scooter
Micah Toll
| Nov 7 2026 - 4:30 am PT
Yamaha is expanding its electric scooter lineup with the new XENTER E, a 125cc-equivalent electric scooter designed specifically with European city riding in mind.
Unveiled around EICMA 2026 in Milan
alongside the new NMAX E
, the XENTER E is a high-wheel scooter riding on 16-inch wheels front and rear.
That’s an important distinction in European cities, where larger wheels can make quick work of the cobblestones, potholes, and tram tracks that can turn smaller-wheeled scooters into teeth-rattling experiences.
The XENTER E uses Yamaha’s new eAxle powertrain, combining the motor, controller, and reduction gearbox into a compact frame-mounted unit. The motor produces 7.5 kW (10 hp) of peak power and 33.3 Nm of torque, putting the scooter into Europe’s A1 license category.
Mounting the motor to the frame also means Yamaha can use a more conventional motorcycle-style swingarm rather than hanging the motor on the rear suspension like many scooters. That reduces unsprung weight and should help improve handling and ride quality.
Power is supplied from an integrated 3.5 kWh battery mounted low in the chassis. Yamaha claims 108 km (67 miles) of range on the WMTC Class 1 cycle, though real-world range is expected to be somewhat lower.
An 800W onboard charger can refill the battery in around 5.5 hours from a public charging station. Yamaha will also offer a cable for charging from a household outlet.
Other niceties include three riding modes, traction control, regenerative braking, a reverse mode for maneuvering at low speeds, smart-key operation, and a 5-inch TFT display. Smartphone connectivity adds navigation, battery information, maintenance reminders, and parking-location tracking.
There’s also enough underseat storage for a full-face helmet, depending on its size, plus USB-C charging and provisions for accessories such as a windscreen and 34-liter top case.
The XENTER E shares its powertrain and battery with
Yamaha’s new NMAX E
, but the high-wheel layout gives it a distinctly more European commuter flavor.
Yamaha hasn’t officially announced pricing for each market, though
early reports
It’s certainly not cheap, but the XENTER E looks like Yamaha is finally getting serious about building electric scooters that can replace its bread-and-butter 125cc urban machines, rather than simply supplement them.

title: Honda just showed off its first high-end electric mountain bike
content:
Micah Toll
| Nov 7 2026 - 3:51 am PT
Honda makes just about everything with a motor, from lawnmowers and generators to cars, motorcycles, and even airplanes. Now the Japanese giant is adding another electrified vehicle to the list – a premium electric mountain bike.
Unveiled at EICMA 2026 in Milan, the new Honda RN0 marks the company’s first entry into the premium electric mountain bike market. And unlike many
automotive-branded e-bikes
that amount to little more than a licensing deal and a familiar logo slapped on someone else’s frame, Honda appears to have actually put some engineering muscle behind this one.
The RN0 was
jointly developed
with German high-end e-MTB manufacturer ROTWILD and features a proprietary carbon monocoque frame and distinctive gull-arm swingarm inspired by Honda’s motorcycle chassis development experience.
There’s actually some real history behind that connection. Honda experimented with mountain bike development in the early 2000s, culminating in its wild RN01 downhill racing bike. In 2005, that project won the overall series championship in the UCI Mountain Bike Downhill World Cup. Honda never turned the RN01 into a consumer bicycle, but more than two decades later, the RN0 is effectively picking up where the company previously left off.
The roughly 24 kg (53 lb) RN0 is set up as a multi-role electric mountain bike, featuring 160 mm FOX 36 FLOAT Factory Kashima front suspension paired with a FOX FLOAT X Factory Kashima rear shock. DT Swiss H1900 SPLINE wheels use a mullet setup with a 29-inch wheel up front and 27.5-inch wheel in the rear, while Shimano DEORE XT four-piston brakes handle stopping duties.
Those are some quality components, but the drivetrain may be even more interesting.
Honda is using Shimano’s new 2.3 kg drive unit, rated for up to 100 Nm of torque and 750 watts of maximum output, paired with a sizeable 720 Wh battery.
Shimano’s AUTO ASSIST can automatically vary motor assistance based on terrain and rider input, while AUTO SHIFT handles gear changes to maintain an appropriate cadence.
There’s even an Assist Carryover function that briefly continues providing power after pedaling stops, potentially making it easier to clear rocks, roots, and other technical obstacles that normally would see the assist grind to a halt right when it is needed most.
A 2.2-inch color display is integrated directly into the top tube, and there’s USB-C charging plus Shimano app connectivity for adjusting motor settings and electronically locking the bike.
hasn’t yet announced
pricing in its release, but with a carbon chassis, Factory-level FOX suspension, XT brakes, and premium Shimano electronics, don’t expect this to be the everyman’s electric bike.
If anything, the RN0 looks much more like Honda is finally bringing its motorcycle engineering mentality back to mountain bikes – this time with a battery and motor along for the ride.

content:
Markets & Policy
With national inventory surging 126% in the second quarter of 2026 ahead of shifting trade cutoffs, utility-scale developers are altering procurement strategies and contracts to manage multi-layered regulatory uncertainty.
Ryan Kennedy
07 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
The Permian Energy Center in Texas
U.S. solar equipment inventories expanded by 126% during the second quarter of 2026 as project developers accelerated procurement to clear a series of federal trade cutoffs.
Developers across the country are working to reconcile overlapping federal policies with distinct regulatory objectives. The industry spent the summer navigating the July 4 construction-start deadline, the July 24 tariff transition, Foreign Entity of Concern restrictions, and Federal Communications Commission rules regarding inverter components. Attention has now turned toward Dec. 4, when new Section 232 measures take effect for polysilicon, wafers, cells, and modules.
For utility-scale solar and energy storage developers, operating in this environment requires restructuring multi-party contracts and building operational flexibility into project financing rather than speculating on spot market prices.
Sabah Bayatli, chief executive officer of San Antonio-based developer OCI Energy, said the market spent late summer and early autumn focused on how Section 232 will dictate post-December pricing dynamics.
Under the Section 232 proclamation, minimum import price thresholds sit at $0.22 per watt for solar cells and $0.38 per watt for finished solar modules.
“Without further guidance from the government, it is hard for the market to price solar modules today, because there are two scenarios for modules post-December 4,” Bayatli told
pv magazine USA
. “It comes down to whether a manufacturer who imports cells from outside the country is able to sell finished panels for less than 38 cents.”
In addition to price floor interpretations, developers are awaiting administrative guidance from federal trade agencies. U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Commerce are expected to issue procedural instructions detailing the self-certification forms importers must execute to clear shipments at entry ports after the deadline.
Equipment delivery schedules for funded projects undergoing active construction remain largely insulated from immediate balance sheet shocks, as hardware for those sites was under contract prior to the proclamation. The primary exposure sits in long-term procurement structures for pipeline projects scheduled for construction in 2027 and beyond.
To absorb regulatory volatility, OCI Energy relies on collaborative contract structures that spread policy risk among project sponsors, equipment vendors, EPC contractors, lenders, and off-takers.
“These multiple stakeholders need to come together through you as a sponsor to make sure there is flexibility on managing future tariffs that you do not have visibility on today,” Bayatli said. “In the contract, you see change in law or change in tariff clauses that allow the developer to share risk across multiple stakeholders so no single entity carries the full exposure.”
When trade policy generates expenses that cannot be absorbed within fixed construction budgets, the cost is ultimately transferred to electricity buyers.
“Eventually, any additional tariffs that you did not bake inside your financial model will flow into the power pricing,” Bayatli said. “What that translates to is having a higher PPA pricing to make the project economically work.”
Despite the friction created by shifting trade mandates, market fundamentals and long-term project pipelines remain firm as developers continuously adapt to regulatory shifts.
“As a developer, you are always on your toes these days,” Bayatli said. “You have to catch up with the market and adjust to regulatory changes, but developers will always find a way to navigate through it.”

title: How the Solar+ industries can make better decisions for the energy transition - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
This week, Women in Solar+ Europe (WiSEu) shares the lessons from its Solar & Storage Live European tour: why silence puts projects at risk, what turns representation into real influence, and how leaders can make room for challenge, learning and innovation, even under pressure.
Women in Solar+ Europe
07 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
The value of a diverse team depends on what happens when its members disagree. Can someone challenge the person in charge? Does their input change a decision? Can they lead change without a senior title? This year, Women in Solar+ Europe (WiSEu) explored these questions at six Solar & Storage Live events across the UK, Spain, Switzerland, Italy and France, bringing together developers and IPPs, investors, consultants, HR and DEI leads, industry associations and innovation teams.
Across these conversations, a clear picture emerged: trust gives people the confidence to speak, genuine participation allows them to shape outcomes, and leadership enables them to act. In solar and storage, where no individual holds the full technical, financial, regulatory and commercial picture, these conditions matter. Creating them requires leaders to welcome uncomfortable perspectives, share information and give people ownership, especially when pressure makes it easier to fall back on familiar voices and established hierarchies.
“‘Inclusion’ has become a buzzword, and some organisations are now stepping back from it. That makes it even more important to be clear about what it means in practice: people being able to challenge assumptions, contribute their expertise, influence decisions and access opportunities fairly. This year, we wanted to bring the conversation back to those daily and organisational practices and how they build stronger teams to meet the challenges of the energy transition. It is easier to surround ourselves with people who think and act like us. Good leadership means becoming comfortable outside our comfort zone, working with people whose perspectives differ from our own and being willing to let them change and evolve our thinking,” says Carmen Madrid, Founder of Women in Solar+ Europe.
The cost of silence
When someone notices a weakness in a proposal but hesitates to raise it, the underlying risk remains. An assumption can become a procurement decision, an investment commitment or a delivery problem.
“When people don’t feel safe to challenge assumptions early, we don’t just lose ideas, we lock in risk, cost, and inefficiencies that show up later in delivery,” explains Jessimiela Usidame, Project Procurement Manager.
Psychological safety is therefore a practical leadership responsibility. People need confidence that asking questions, acknowledging uncertainty or flagging mistakes will lead to constructive discussion.
Leaders build that confidence through repeated behaviours. Admitting uncertainty and thanking colleagues who identify errors gives others permission to do the same. Speaking last can prevent a senior opinion from setting the boundaries before others contribute.
Trust creates space for challenge
Teams need to distinguish between challenging an idea and undermining its author. Respectful scrutiny helps people expose gaps and improve proposals while maintaining accountability.
“Psychological safety does not eliminate conflict; it allows disagreement to become a tool for making better decisions,” reflects Kim Keats Martínez, Managing Partner at EKON Strategy Consulting.
Putting this into practice requires leaders to be willing to be challenged themselves. Jesús Alijarde, Founder and Director General of Ibersyd, described growing trust through colleagues’ confidence to tell him: “Jesús, it’s your company, but I think you’re getting this wrong.” For him, hearing those words is a source of pride: evidence that people feel safe enough to question the person in charge.
Participation means shaping the outcome
Confidence to speak must be accompanied by information and opportunities to influence decisions. People need relevant context, clear objectives and an understanding of where their contribution can make a difference.
Who defines the problem also matters. Before a team is invited to suggest solutions, choices may already have been made about priorities and assumptions. Bringing different perspectives into that earlier stage can change the question itself.
“Real influence happens while you are producing the deliverable, while you are bringing people together around it, rather than when you are merely ‘consulted’,” explains Floriane de Brabandère, President of FNES.
Drafting proposals, coordinating working groups and leading pilots provide opportunities to shape outcomes. These responsibilities should extend beyond familiar senior or highly visible colleagues.
People also need to see how their input influenced a decision, understand why an idea was declined and receive recognition when a contribution moves forward. Feedback without follow-through gradually teaches people to disengage.
Innovation needs room to learn
Innovation requires opportunities to discover what works when outcomes are uncertain. Small, protected trials with clear boundaries can generate evidence while managing financial exposure. “Psychological safety becomes tangible when people move from ‘I cannot make a mistake’ to ‘I can learn’,” explains Filipa Monteiro Martins, Renewable Innovation Unit Manager at Galp.
Leaders need to distinguish between operational delivery and exploration. A pilot that reveals why an approach will fail can provide valuable learning. Evaluating every experiment against immediate commercial returns encourages safe proposals and limits discovery. Clear expectations about what is being tested, acceptable risks and how learning will inform the next decision allow teams to experiment responsibly.
Making participation an everyday practice
Alongside organisational responsibility sits individual agency. People need encouragement to use their expertise, offer alternatives and help develop solutions. Shared purpose gives that initiative direction. “Empowerment means trusting people to take ownership and influence change without needing a senior job title or endless layers of approval,” says Hollie Carek, Head of UK at OpenSolar.
These practices also strengthen collaboration across organisations and generations, connecting different experiences to the challenges the industry shares.
“The energy transition needs leaders who enable people from different backgrounds and generations to contribute, learn from one another and influence decisions. When we combine that diversity of experience with trust, shared purpose and opportunities to progress, we build the collective intelligence to move our industry forward,” concludes Nadia Lalout-Landemaine, Advisor and Consultant at PaceUP Invest and WiSEu panel moderator.
Putting inclusive leadership into practice
Shaped by hours of conversations across this year’s tour, our final event of the year will turn these insights into practice. The
WiSEu Breakfast Workshop during Genera
in Madrid on Wednesday 25 November, “Leading Beyond Stereotypes: Strategies for Participation, Recognition and Career Progression,” will be fully interactive. Through practical scenarios and facilitated roundtables, participants from our Spanish and International community will explore how to make their voices heard, ensure contributions are recognised fairly and access opportunities to progress, leaving with strategies for their careers and for creating fairer opportunities within their teams. Allies are welcome.

title: Ecuador's largest PV plant goes online - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Lighthouse, a subsidiary of Ecuador’s Difare Group, has inaugurated an 82 MW solar plant in Santa Elena province.
Luis Ini
07 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Americas
Utility-scale
Lighthouse, a subsidiary of industrial conglomerate Difare Group, inaugurated the 82 MW Faro de San Marcos solar plant on Nov. 5.
The facility, located in Baños de San Vicente, in Ecuador’s Santa Elena province, has entered commercial operation and features more than 105,000 bifacial solar modules. According to the developer, it is Ecuador’s largest operational and privately owned solar power plant.
The project spans 49.3 hectares and required an investment of $50 million in its first phase. Construction took eight months and employed an average of 400 workers.
According to technical information released during project development, the installation features fixed-tilt, dual-slope mounting structures, string inverters and transformer stations. Its installed capacity exceeds the 75 MW initially planned when the company announced the project in December 2025.
Lighthouse expects the plant to generate approximately 106 GWh of electricity annually, equivalent to the consumption of around 15,000 households, according to company estimates. The electricity will be delivered through the distribution network operated by Ecuador’s state-owned utility Corporación Nacional de Electricidad (CNEL EP).
Initial electricity customers include Corporación El Rosado, retail chain Tía and Difare. The project enables these companies to source solar electricity through the existing grid without installing PV systems at their own facilities.
Commercial operations have begun ahead of the original schedule, which called for commissioning in the first quarter of 2027. Lighthouse Península, established in Ecuador in 2024 and incorporated into the Difare Group in 2025, is pursuing further solar development. During the inauguration, Difare Group Executive Chairman Carlos Cueva Mejía announced plans for another project on adjacent land, with an estimated investment of $80 million.
The commissioning adds to a growing number of privately developed solar projects in Ecuador. In Santa Elena province, the 65 MW Río de Oro Energy solar plant began supplying electricity to commercial customers in September. Developed by GPS Group, the project represents an investment of more than $50 million and is expected to generate approximately 90 GWh annually.
Ecuador has been seeking to accelerate private investment in renewable energy following the electricity shortages and widespread blackouts of 2024. In August 2025, the government had authorized
643 MW of private renewable energy projects, including solar and hydropower
. The total comprised 179.1 MW of distributed generation projects intended to supply the electricity market and 464.6 MW of self-generation capacity for corporate consumers, with the option to sell surplus electricity.
According to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), Ecuador had 131.35 MW of cumulative installed solar PV capacity at the end of 2025, up from approximately 84 MW in 2024.
