title: Maintaining trust in new tech - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Rapid technological advances, particularly in AI, are challenging traditional approaches to conformity assessment and standardization. International standards bodies are adapting their frameworks to ensure products remain safe, reliable and trustworthy throughout their lifecycles.
International Electrotechnical Commission (ICE)
07 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Standards are often invisible to the people who rely on them, yet they underpin the confidence that products will work together, operate safely and perform as expected. But rapid technological change resulting from digitalization and the widespread use of AI is challenging traditional ways of assessing conformity to standards.
“Standardization and confirmity assessment (CA) bring tremendous value by providing trust in new technology,” says Wolfram Zeitz, executive secretary of two of the IEC CA systems, IECEE, which is the IEC System of Conformity Assessment Schemes for Electrotechnical Equipment and Components, and IECRE, which is the IEC System for Certification to Standards Relating to Equipment for Use in Renewable Energy Applications.
“What has changed is the speed of development. In the past, product cycles took up to three years before prototypes appeared,” he adds. “Now change happens far, far quicker and this creates a feeling of uncertainty. Consumers lose trust when they think development was rushed and conformity is not being adhered to.”
Henrike Gördes, head of governance at DKE, the organization hosting this year’s IEC general meeting, agrees: “A product that conforms to relevant standards provides assurance that it will behave in predictable ways and interact appropriately within a wider technological ecosystem. This ability to create trust has been one of the foundations of the success of standardization over many years. But maintaining that trust is becoming more challenging as technology changes at an accelerating pace.”
The potential undermining of a standards-based order is particularly acute when software, data or AI can alter a product’s behavior. The question is no longer simply whether the product was safe when it was tested. It is also how organizations can ensure that it remains safe and operates as intended following updates, changes in data or advances in AI, which are happening faster and faster.
Keeping pace with AI
The problem with attempting to standardize systems and products in an emerging environment is that the technology may not be mature enough to stabilize. “Particularly for AI, we don’t yet have industrial consensus on the technological framework,” says Zeitz. “AI tools are using different technological setups almost daily. Standardization and conformity assessment are struggling to keep up with the speed of development.”
Progress is being made, however. CASCO, the ISO committee for CA, is working with ISO/IEC SC 42 on ISO/IEC 42007, a draft standard offering a high-level framework and guidance for the development of CA schemes for AI systems.
Cybersecurity is one of the challenges related to AI, and in this area the IECEE Industrial Cyber Security Programme, which is based on the IEC 62443 series of standards, is already well established. A new pilot CA program has also recently been initiated with IEC TC 62, the technical committee that prepares standards for medical devices, to look at how AI can be assessed.
All new technologies need to be trusted
While AI is very much the focus of global attention, a host of new technologies required in our evolving world – notably to meet net-zero targets – also require standards and CA to be used safely and effectively. Different countries around the world need to trust that manufacturers providing the technology and products meet the appropriate benchmarks.
The difference is that these technologies are not evolving at the same pace as AI-based systems and are therefore easier to assess. For instance, IECEE provides a testing and certification scheme for electric vehicle (EV) battery systems, assessing their safety, performance, interoperability, energy efficiency, electromagnetic compatibility and hazardous substances. It also operates a specific EV program, which can test and certify charging systems, stations and plugs against relevant IEC standards, including IEC 62196-1 and the IEC 61851 series.
IECEE is also the go-to body for ensuring that solar panels and components are safe and perform as planned through its national certification bodies and recognized testing laboratories. The system relies on IEC standards for module performance, durability and safety. IEC 61215 covers design qualification and type approval of terrestrial photovoltaic modules, while IEC 61730 addresses electrical and mechanical safety through construction and testing requirements.
IECRE was established a little more than 10 years ago to help provide third-party certification and testing services for all power plants producing, storing or converting energy from wind, marine and solar PV energy. The CA system ensures that the essential quality and safety requirements in standards are met and, as a consequence, that reliable performance can be expected from all these systems.
For the wind sector, for example, that means checking that the industry aligns with the IEC 61400 standards, developed by IEC TC 88, the technical committee that produces standards for wind energy systems.
Conformity assessment is evolving
Traditionally, CA has often followed a relatively linear model: a product is developed, tested and assessed, and then the assessment provides assurance about that product. Digital and AI-based technologies complicate this.
“Take the introduction of autonomous control in cars, for example. You could have a software update that basically changes the way the self-driving vehicle operates,” says Gördes.
This raises an important question for conformity assessment: What does it mean to demonstrate that a product remains safe and performs as intended when the product itself can continue to change?
“Rather than assessing a product only at a particular point in its development, assessment needs to take account of what happens throughout the product’s lifecycle,” Gördes says.
DKE advocates a shift from a linear model of CA toward a more continuous, cyclical approach. “Such an approach could help connect CA more closely with the reality of digital products, where development, deployment, updating and monitoring can form an ongoing process rather than a sequence that ends when a product is first assessed.”
The aim, as outlined in this DKE white paper, is to develop an approach that better reflects products and technologies that can change throughout their operational life.
DKE is working with stakeholders from different industries and in cooperation with DIN and VDE, Germany’s national standards bodies, to develop the concept. “DKE has a strong interest in ensuring that emerging thinking can ultimately contribute to international standardization,” Gördes says.
Independent assessment is essential to ensure trust
The international dimension matters because standards and CA operate across markets. Manufacturers, regulators and users need confidence that assurance mechanisms are meaningful not only within individual national systems but also across increasingly global technology ecosystems.
“Our entire framework of requirements is based on international agreements and consensus,” explains Zeitz. “Every member country, no matter how big or small, has the same voting rights. The voice of Germany or the US has the same weight as Kenya. This is embedded in our governance and this matters because the community and the public need to know that a requirement – whether technical or procedural – is not just the opinion of one party. International agreement and consensus building is a strong factor in trust.”
“Only third-party assessment gives full independence,” Zeitz insists. “That’s why our CA systems rely on completely impartial laboratories, certification or inspection bodies. Only such a set-up can give the market full trust and confidence in the safety, efficiency and interoperability of the different products.”
The International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) is a global, not-for-profit membership organization that brings together 174 countries and coordinates the work of 30.000 experts globally. IEC International Standards and conformity assessment underpin international trade in electrical and electronic goods. They facilitate electricity access and verify the safety, performance and interoperability of electric and electronic devices and systems, including for example, consumer devices such as mobile phones or refrigerators, office and medical equipment, information technology, electricity generation, and much more.

title: Portable solar-powered system produces 1.64 liters of drinking water in 8 hours - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers at Soochow University in China have developed a portable solar-powered system that converts saline, turbid and contaminated water into drinking water using an electrothermal evaporator and concentrated sunlight. The device produced 1.64 liters of clean water in eight hours, achieving an energy efficiency of 93.31%.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
07 Nov 2026
Research & Development
A research team from
Soochow University
in China has developed a portable solar-powered device that produces drinking water from turbid, saline, oily and highly acidic water. The prototype produced 1.64 liters of clean water in eight hours using an evaporation surface measuring just 30.72 cm2.
The system uses an electrothermal evaporation process in which an electrically powered heating element heats a surface that absorbs contaminated water, causing the water to evaporate. The resulting vapor is collected and condensed into clean water, while salts and other contaminants remain in the source water.
The device’s main innovation is an interlayer electrothermal evaporator. Instead of heating the entire volume of the wet material, the researchers positioned the heating element within an internal layer of the structure.
This configuration reduces heat losses to the surrounding water and air. According to the study, the design reduced heat losses and energy consumption by nearly two-thirds compared with a conventional electrothermal evaporator based on volumetric heating.
The system also combines two sources of solar energy.
It features foldable solar cells that generate electricity to power the electrothermal evaporator, alongside a foldable Fresnel lens that concentrates sunlight directly onto the evaporation surface. The study does not specify the rated capacity or electrical characteristics of the PV system.
When accounting for concentrated solar energy, the device achieved an apparent energy efficiency of 93.31% and a water production rate of 69.46 liters per square meter per hour.
Outdoor tests showed that the prototype could produce 1.64 liters of drinking water in eight hours using an evaporation surface of 30.72 cm2, smaller than a standard bank card.
The researchers tested the system with different types of water, including sediment-laden water, oil-contaminated water, highly saline wastewater and strongly acidic water.
The tests also included real seawater, with the researchers analyzing water samples before and after treatment. Under concentrated sunlight, the system achieved evaporation rates exceeding 90 kg/m2 per hour.
The device integrates PV modules and an optical solar concentration system, allowing it to operate without a grid connection or external fuel supply. The researchers said the configuration could be used in areas where conventional water supply infrastructure is damaged or unavailable.
They also suggested that the technology could serve as a portable water treatment solution in emergencies, including floods, earthquakes and conflicts, where access to safe drinking water may be disrupted.
The researchers presented their findings in “
Solar-operated interlayer electrothermal evaporator enabling instant high-flux freshwater production across multiple scenarios
,” published in
Nature Water
. Outdoor tests were conducted using a small-scale prototype on selected days in January and February 2025.
The results demonstrate the feasibility of the concept, but larger systems and longer-term testing under real-world conditions are still needed to assess its potential for large-scale deployment.

title: Researchers develop 10.56 kW solar-powered pleasure boat - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in Canada have designed a solar-powered pleasure boat featuring a 10.56 kW PV array and a 19.68 kWh battery system. Simulations under solar conditions in Cyprus showed that the system could meet propulsion demand while providing a 39.8% surplus energy margin.
Lior Kahana
07 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Residential
The proposed pleasure boat
A research team from Canada’s Memorial University of Newfoundland has designed a solar-powered pleasure boat. The researchers developed and sized the system using a two-stage evaluation method combining energy yield estimates from HOMER Pro with multi-domain dynamic modeling in MATLAB/Simulink.
“The real-world applicability of this solar-electric drive system underscores significant environmental and operational benefits for the marine sector,” the researchers said. “By eliminating onboard fossil-fuel consumption, the proposed architecture avoids localized greenhouse gas emissions, reduces acoustic pollution, and prevents potential fuel-spill contamination in fragile marine ecosystems.”
The researchers designed the solar-electric propulsion system for an 11.8-meter-long, 5.8-meter-wide boat capable of accommodating five to six adults, taking into account solar conditions in Larnaca, Cyprus. Based on a full-load displacement of approximately 2,250 kg and a target speed of 5.4 knots, they selected two 2.5 kW brushless DC motors, with an estimated energy requirement of 30 kWh for six hours of daily operation.
Using HOMER Pro and local solar resource data showing average daily irradiation of 5.43 kWh/m2, the researchers assessed power generation, energy balance and life-cycle economics. The proposed system features 32 solar modules rated at 330 W each, providing a combined capacity of 10.56 kW across approximately 62.4 m2. The modules are divided into four independently controlled subarrays. Eight lead-acid batteries form a 48 V, 410 Ah battery bank with a nominal storage capacity of 19.68 kWh, providing two hours of backup power.
The team modeled the system in MATLAB/Simulink, connecting each subarray to a common 48 V DC bus through a boost converter equipped with incremental-conductance maximum power point tracking (MPPT). A central energy management system limits battery charging current to approximately 50 A and curtails surplus generation. Hall-effect sensors and closed-loop proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control regulate motor speed at 2,000 rpm. The simulations covered solar-only, combined PV-battery and battery-only operating modes, assessing power tracking, voltage stability and motor response.
“Dynamic simulation results under localized clear-sky irradiance peaks confirm that the decentralized PV system achieves a maximum output of nearly 10.98 kW,” the researchers said. “Evaluated against the logical profiles of Larnaca, Cyprus, the array fully satisfies the baseline propulsion demand while delivering a robust 39.8% excess energy margin.”
The results also showed that the four incremental-conductance MPPT controllers effectively minimized power-tracking oscillations, while the energy management system maintained DC-bus voltage fluctuations within ±3% of the nominal 48 V rating.
“While this simulation-based work establishes a rigorous computational foundation for system control and dynamic sizing, several avenues remain for future development,” the researchers concluded. “Furthermore, experimental validation through physical full-scale sea trials could be conducted to verify real-world hydrodynamic drag effects, alongside detailed techno-economic sensitivity analyses evaluating levelized cost of energy (LCOE), net present cost (NPC), capital paybacks, and cycle degradation under fluctuating market interest rates and fuel prices.”
The researchers presented their findings in “
Integrated modeling and performance assessment of a stand-alone PV-battery system for a solar-powered pleasure boat
,” published in
Next Research

title: Study finds 0.5-meter spacing between solar module rows improves cooling in floating PV systems - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
A study by Italian researchers has found that 0.5-meter spacing between module rows optimizes cooling in floating PV systems by improving airflow. The findings highlight the importance of row spacing in thermal management, although further research is needed to assess its impact on electricity generation.
Sergio Matalucci
07 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Floating PV
Utility-scale
A computational fluid dynamics study of a proposed floating PV installation at the Occhito Dam reservoir in southern Italy has found that spacing module rows approximately 0.5 meters apart delivers the best cooling performance in a three-row configuration. The researchers found that the intermediate spacing outperformed both narrower and wider arrangements, highlighting the importance of airflow management in floating PV system design.
At a wind speed of 3.5 m/s, the optimal configuration achieved an average module temperature of 27.16 C, compared with 31.07 C for the most compact arrangement. Under weaker wind conditions of 1.5 m/s, the same configuration recorded an average module temperature of 37.02 C.
The study notes that the efficiency of crystalline silicon PV modules typically decreases by approximately 0.3% to 0.5% for every 1 C increase in cell temperature. The findings underscore the importance of airflow management in floating PV design and challenge the assumption that proximity to water alone ensures better cooling.
The researchers said row spacing should be considered not only in terms of installed capacity, shading, and floating platform requirements, but also as a key thermal design parameter.
The research, conducted by scientists from the University of Naples Parthenope and the University of Campania Luigi Vanvitelli, also identified a less intuitive aspect of floating PV cooling. Although the widest spacing allowed airflow to recover more fully between rows, it did not consistently produce the lowest module temperatures. The researchers attributed this to reduced airflow acceleration between rows.
The findings suggest that effective cooling requires a balance between aerodynamic wake recovery and airflow acceleration, with the optimal configuration depending on site-specific conditions.
Airflow acceleration and differences between module rows
Cooling performance depends on several interacting factors, including wind speed, array geometry, airflow pathways, and the formation of aerodynamic wakes behind individual module rows.
These wakes can restrict air movement around the modules, reducing convective heat transfer and increasing operating temperatures. While greater row spacing can allow airflow to recover before reaching the next module, wider gaps do not necessarily improve cooling. The researchers found that excessive spacing can weaken airflow acceleration between rows.
At a wind speed of 1.5 m/s, spacing equivalent to 0.5 times the module length delivered the best performance, with an average module temperature of 37.02 C. The widest configuration, with spacing equal to one module length, performed worst, reaching 37.74 C.
The differences became more pronounced at 3.5 m/s. The configuration with spacing equivalent to 0.5 times the module length recorded an average temperature of 27.16 C, compared with 29.26 C for spacing of 0.75 times the module length, 29.75 C for the widest arrangement, and 31.07 C for the most compact configuration.
The study also found that cooling performance varied between module rows. The middle row was particularly sensitive to changes in spacing.
At 3.5 m/s, the middle row reached a temperature of 23.30 C with spacing equivalent to 0.5 times the module length, compared with 29.66 C in the most compact configuration and 30.17 C in the widest arrangement. According to the researchers, this behavior reflects the middle row’s exposure to the competing effects of upstream wake formation and airflow recovery.
The simulations also showed that the relationship between row spacing and module temperature is nonlinear. An analysis of airflow velocities under different operating conditions helped explain these differences.
At the lower wind speed, airflow velocity between the first two rows remained below 0.5 m/s in the most compact configuration. Increasing the spacing to 0.5 times the module length raised local airflow velocity to approximately 0.9 m/s to 1.1 m/s.
At the higher wind speed, the difference was even more pronounced. The intermediate spacing produced airflow velocities between rows of approximately 2.5 m/s to 3.0 m/s, compared with 1.0 m/s to 1.5 m/s for the most compact arrangement.
Four configurations
The researchers developed a two-dimensional conjugate heat transfer model to simulate interactions between PV modules, the surrounding air, and the underlying water.
The proposed installation was modeled using three consecutive rows of modules, each tilted at 15 degrees and positioned 25 cm above the water surface. The modules were approximately 0.99 meters long.
Four row-spacing configurations were examined, corresponding to 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1.0 times the module length. The simulations considered two incoming wind speeds, 1.5 m/s and 3.5 m/s, representing relatively weak and stronger convective cooling conditions.
Meteorological inputs were derived from hourly ERA5 reanalysis data for 2024 covering the Occhito reservoir, which lies on the border between the Italian regions of Apulia and Molise.
The model used an annual average air temperature of 15.37 C, a water temperature of 14.67 C, and a net shortwave radiation flux of 146.65 W/m2.
Further research needed
The findings are particularly relevant to inland reservoirs in Mediterranean climates, where high summer temperatures and variable wind conditions can affect PV module operating temperatures.
However, the researchers cautioned against treating the identified spacing as a universal design recommendation.
The analysis was limited to a two-dimensional model comprising three module rows and two wind speeds. It did not account for three-dimensional turbulence, changes in wind direction, shading effects, detailed floating support structures, or the full range of meteorological conditions experienced over a year.
The study, “
Influence of row spacings on the thermal performance of floating photovoltaic arrays at the Occhito Dam reservoir, Italy: A numerical study
,” published in
Solar Energy
, focused on thermal behavior rather than directly calculating electricity generation or annual energy yield.
The authors recommended extending the research through three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics simulations, additional wind speeds and directions, and integrated electrothermal modeling to determine how the observed temperature differences translate into actual electricity generation gains.

title: India’s installed solar PV capacity to exceed 350 GW by 2030, says IEA - pv magazine Global
政策分类路径: 政策 > 战略规划型政策 > 规划目标
政策分类依据: IEA报告提出印度2030年350GW光伏、500GW非化石能源装机等定量目标
content:
Markets & Policy
Growth will be supported by utility-scale projects, rooftop solar and corporate procurement, although grid and storage investments remain critical.
Uma Gupta
07 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
A solar power plant in the Indian state of Maharashtra
India’s installed solar PV capacity is expected to exceed 350 GW by 2030, according to the IEA’s India Renewable Energy Market Report 2026.
The report, launched at the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit in New Delhi, forecasts that India’s total installed renewable power capacity will reach around 530 GW by 2030, with solar PV accounting for the largest share of growth. Wind capacity is expected to approach 90 GW, while hydropower capacity is projected to reach 75 GW as large hydro projects come online and investment in pumped storage accelerates.
The expansion is expected to put India on track to meet its target of 500 GW of installed non-fossil fuel power capacity by 2030, a key milestone toward its goal of achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2070.
Competitive costs, sustained auction activity, growing open-access procurement and accelerating rooftop installations are expected to drive solar PV deployment.
Utility-scale projects have accounted for around 75% of solar PV capacity additions over the past five years. The IEA expects that share to gradually decline to approximately 70% by 2030, as policy support, improving economics and simplified administrative procedures boost distributed solar deployment.
Distributed solar PV capacity for self-consumption is projected to triple to more than 100 GW by 2030. The PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana scheme is accelerating residential rooftop installations, while PM-KUSUM supports the solarization of agricultural feeders and irrigation pumps.
Corporate procurement is also emerging as a major source of demand. Open-access reforms have simplified renewable energy procurement for commercial and industrial consumers, with corporate power purchase agreements expected to support around 20% of utility-scale solar PV and wind capacity additions by 2030.
India’s installed renewable power capacity has almost quadrupled over the past decade, surpassing 300 GW in 2026, according to the report. The country is now the world’s second-fastest-growing renewable energy market and second-largest solar module manufacturer. India also reached its target of 50% non-fossil fuel installed power capacity in 2025, five years ahead of schedule.
The IEA said renewable energy deployment is already delivering substantial energy security benefits. Renewable electricity saved India more than $100 billion in coal and natural gas import costs between 2011 and 2025, with cumulative savings expected to more than double by 2030. Without the solar PV, wind and bioenergy capacity added since 2010, India’s coal imports in 2025 would have been around 110 million metric tons higher.
“India’s renewables expansion is delivering major benefits for its energy security at a time of heightened uncertainty in global energy markets,” said IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol. “As countries look to strengthen domestic energy supplies, India’s experience shows how consistent policies can help drive down renewable energy costs and attract investment, offering valuable lessons for other emerging economies. We look forward to supporting India as it builds on these achievements.”
“India’s emergence as a new giant of renewable energy reflects the progress we have made in recent years,” said India’s Minister of New and Renewable Energy Pralhad Joshi. “As India’s electricity needs continue to rise, we are laying the foundations for the next phase of growth by strengthening domestic manufacturing, mobilising investment and expanding transmission infrastructure.”
The report said competitive auctions have helped India achieve some of the world’s lowest solar PV generation costs and become a global leader in procuring hybrid renewable energy projects. Growth is also extending beyond utility-scale power plants, supported by rooftop solar, corporate electricity procurement and expanding domestic manufacturing.
However, sustaining the expansion will require faster investment in electricity grids, energy storage and system flexibility, alongside stronger utility finances and fewer project delays. Addressing these challenges could accelerate renewable power capacity deployment by more than 20% between 2026 and 2030, according to the IEA.

title: Beyond scale and hardware - pv magazine Global
content: Starting points may be different for solar and BESS, but the strategic challenges are converging. Manufacturing scale remains important, but hardware alone is becoming less of a competitive differentiator. With margins already under pressure, the window to reposition is narrowing. The question becomes, where can manufacturers capture value beyond equipment? Since 2015, total installed solar capacity has increased around 13-fold, from 220 GW to 2.7 TW in 2026, while BESS capacity has grown more than 200-fold, from 2.2 GW in 2015 to around 470 GW in 2026. By 2035, cumulative capacity is on track to exceed 8 TW for solar and 2.4 TW for BESS. Solar is already deep into an oversupply cycle. Global module manufacturing capacity exceeded 1.1 TW in 2025, nearly twice annual demand. Tier-1 PV module manufacturers responded by cutting production, with average utilization rates falling from 75% in 2023 to around 60% in 2026. Lower utilization increased unit costs just as intense price competition eroded margins. Slower Chinese demand in 2026 has added further pressure. BESS manufacturing, on the other hand, is still in a strong growth phase. Deployment is growing rapidly, supported by falling costs, grid reliability needs, renewables integration and emerging AI data center demand. That growth is still absorbing new capacity entering the market. But the gap is narrowing, manufacturing capacity is expanding rapidly, particularly in China, while cells and storage hardware are already facing stronger price competition. BESS is not yet where solar is today, but some of the same pressures are emerging. Manufacturing advantage China’s scale and integrated supply chains have helped lower solar and battery costs, but rapid capacity expansion has also intensified competition. Tier-1 companies accounted for 83% of global solar module shipments in 2025, compared with 62% for BESS, with the top five accounting for 58% and 42%, respectively (see chart p.21). BESS remains more fragmented because suppliers can still differentiate through technology, safety, software, and integration. But as cells and standardized hardware commoditize, differentiation is also shifting beyond the battery itself. Profitability pressures Market leadership does not necessarily translate into financial strength. Solar shows how quickly the economics can turn: rapid market growth drove aggressive manufacturing expansion, lifting average Tier-1 revenue to more than three times its 2018 level by 2023. But as capacity began to run ahead of demand, oversupply pushed prices down and revenue fell. For solar, these economics are difficult to sustain, particularly when manufacturers sacrifice margins to defend market share. For BESS, the challenge is to preserve profitability as the market matures. For both, strategy is shifting toward three areas: geography, integrated offerings and new sources of demand. Solar diversification Solar manufacturers are reaching the limits of a scale-first strategy. Geography is one answer. Expanding into emerging markets can diversify sales and open new sources of demand, although competition is rising as more suppliers pursue the same opportunity. Protected markets offer another route. In the United States and India, manufacturers are expanding locally to benefit from domestic manufacturing policies and greater protection from imports. Localization can support higher margins and market access, but the advantage can shift as quickly as the policies supporting it. The other answer is to sell more than solar. A notable shift is underway among some Chinese manufacturers, evident even in their names. JA Solar has become simply “JA”, while JinkoSolar is proposing to become “Jinko Holdings.” The rebranding reflects a broader move beyond modules into storage and integrated energy solutions. Moving into adjacent technologies brings a different set of challenges. BESS is already a crowded market and requires capabilities many solar manufacturers lack. Partnerships and acquisitions offer a faster route in, while companies within larger energy or industrial groups have an advantage if they can draw on expertise already available elsewhere in the business. Inevitably not all will successfully make this transition. Storage differentiation BESS manufacturers start from a stronger position because more of the system can still provide differentiation. Cell technology and system design remain important, but value is moving toward software, cybersecurity, energy management systems and the overall integrated offering. The strategic question is how suppliers can capture more of that value before competition catches up. One opportunity already being pursued is deeper system integration. Battery cell manufacturers have increasingly been moving downstream from cells and battery modules into complete BESS solutions, giving them greater control over technology, supply, and cost. Moving the other way is harder: system integrators face the capital and technical barriers of cell manufacturing and typically remain exposed to third-party battery prices and project execution risk. Other value pools remain closer to the cell. Scaled manufacturers such as CATL, BYD, LG Energy Solution and Gotion are better positioned to commercialize new battery chemistries. Another opportunity is to follow where demand is growing fastest. AI data centers play directly to BESS strengths, in fast deployment, reliability and power quality. OEMs are already adapting: Fluence Energy has secured master supply agreements with two major hyperscalers, while CATL is investing in data-center power infrastructure. Future leaders The next generation of leaders may look less like equipment manufacturers and more like energy technology platforms, combining competitive hardware with software, services and integrated energy solutions. The real test will be which companies can expand beyond hardware without sacrificing profitability. The post Beyond scale and hardware appeared first on pv magazine Global .

title: How modern chips work: 10 essential semiconductor technologies explained
content: Modern chips depend on technologies that control electrical current, store information, and move data between components. Their performance reflects advances in transistor design, manufacturing precision, materials, and packaging.These developments support everything from smartphones and computers to electric vehicles and data centers. Here are 10 important semiconductor technologies, how they work, and why they matter.1. FinFET transistorsFinFETs are transistors with narrow silicon channels shaped like upright fins rather than flat structures. A gate wraps around three sides of each fin, controlling the electrical current flowing through it.This design improves control over unwanted current leakage as transistors become smaller. FinFETs helped manufacturers increase performance and energy efficiency across generations of smartphone, computer, and server processors.2. Gate-all-around transistorsGate-all-around transistors surround the current-carrying channel with a gate on every side. Implementations can use thin silicon nanosheets or nanoribbons stacked vertically, with Intel’s RibbonFET providing one example.The surrounding gate offers tighter control over current flow, helping address the challenges of further transistor scaling. Engineers can also adjust channel width to balance performance, power consumption, and the space occupied by a device.3. Extreme ultraviolet lithographyExtreme ultraviolet lithography uses light with a wavelength of 13.5 nanometers to transfer circuit patterns onto a light-sensitive coating on semiconductor wafers. The process requires specialized mirrors and a vacuum environment because EUV light is readily absorbed by many materials.EUV enables finer patterning and can reduce the number of patterning steps required for certain chip layers. High numerical aperture EUV improves optical resolution further, although neither its wavelength nor a process-node name directly describes every transistor dimension.4. Atomic layer deposition and etchingAtomic layer deposition builds extremely thin material films through sequential, controlled surface reactions. Atomic layer etching uses a complementary sequence that modifies a surface and then removes the modified material.These techniques help manufacturers coat complex structures and remove material with precise control. That precision is increasingly important for three-dimensional devices, where small variations can affect electrical behavior and manufacturing consistency.5. Backside power deliveryBackside power delivery routes electrical power through the opposite side of the wafer from the frontside signal connections. This separates two wiring networks that traditionally competed for space above the transistors.The arrangement can ease routing congestion and improve how power reaches densely packed devices. Intel’s PowerVia is one implementation, although manufacturing such structures requires additional processing, including wafer thinning and precise backside connections.6. Chiplets and advanced packagingChiplet designs divide a system’s functions among smaller semiconductor dies connected within a single package. Different dies can handle computing, memory, or input and output, using manufacturing processes suited to their individual requirements.Advanced packaging provides the dense connections that allow these components to operate together, either side by side or in vertical stacksThis approach offers design flexibility and component reuse, while making communication overhead, testing, cost, and heat management important engineering considerations.7. High-bandwidth memoryHigh-bandwidth memory stacks multiple DRAM dies vertically and connects them through dense interconnects, including through-silicon vias. The stacks sit close to a processor and use a wide interface to transfer many bits in parallel.This arrangement helps supply data to demanding workloads such as AI processing and scientific computing. HBM serves as working memory and requires power to retain information, distinguishing it from persistent storage technologies such as NAND flash.8. 3D NAND flash memory3D NAND increases storage density by arranging memory cells across multiple vertical layers within a die. This approach extends capacity beyond what manufacturers could achieve through shrinking a flat arrangement of cells alone.Unlike DRAM, NAND flash retains stored information when power is removed, making it suitable for solid-state drives and other storage products. Its performance and endurance depend on factors beyond layer count, including bits per cell, controller design, and error correction.9. Silicon carbide and gallium nitrideSilicon carbide and gallium nitride are wide-bandgap semiconductor materials used to control and convert electrical power. Their properties offer advantages in applications that require efficient switching, high power density, or high-voltage operation.Silicon carbide is widely used in applications such as electric vehicle inverters, while gallium nitride supports compact, fast-switching power converters.The materials are not interchangeable, and engineers choose between them according to voltage, frequency, thermal requirements, reliability, and cost.10. Silicon photonicsSilicon photonics integrates optical components onto semiconductor platforms to transmit information using light. Waveguides channel the light, modulators encode data, and photodetectors convert incoming optical signals into electrical signals.The technology helps address bandwidth, distance, and energy constraints in communications and computing infrastructure. Its role in optical interconnects complements electronic processing by improving how data travels between components and systems.ConclusionSemiconductor progress depends on coordinated improvements across transistors, manufacturing processes, memory, connections, and power devices. Each technology addresses a different constraint on what electronic systems can accomplish.Smaller switches need precise fabrication, powerful processors need fast data access, and compact power systems need suitable materials. Together, these developments enable engineers to improve performance, capacity, and efficiency across modern electronics.

title: Non-flammable membrane helps fluoride-ion batteries pass 50 cycles
content: Researchers in Italy have developed a polymer membrane that allows fluoride ions to move through a battery electrolyte at room temperature, addressing a major obstacle to the development of next-generation fluoride-ion batteries.The quasi-solid gel membrane, developed by a team at Politecnico di Milano, acts as a fluoride-exchange membrane (FEM), transporting fluoride ions between battery electrodes. The researchers say the approach could help advance an alternative battery chemistry that does not rely on lithium.Fluoride-ion batteries have attracted interest because fluoride is an abundant element and their conversion-based chemistry offers the potential for high energy density. However, developing electrolytes that can transport fluoride ions efficiently at room temperature has remained a significant challenge.The study introduces a polymer electrolyte based on a perfluorosulfonic amide ionomer containing tetraalkylammonium fluoride groups.Membrane enables ion transportTo improve the movement of fluoride ions, the researchers modified the polymer membrane using a mixture of two solvents, 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). The solvent mixture causes the ionomer to swell, creating conditions that allow fluoride ions to move through the quasi-solid material.Measurements using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy showed that the membrane achieved ionic conductivity of up to 1.3 millisiemens per centimeter at room temperature.The team also used molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how the membrane’s structure and solvent composition influence fluoride-ion movement. The simulations indicated that DMSO plays an important role as a polar swelling agent.The researchers then tested the electrolyte in experimental coin cells using lead and lead fluoride electrodes. The cells demonstrated reversible fluorination and defluorination, the processes through which fluoride ions move into and out of electrode materials during charging and discharging.The experiments showed stable cycling over more than 50 cycles at room temperature, with a current density of 0.1C.Lithium-free batteries remain distantThe researchers describe the membrane as the first fluoride-exchange membrane developed for this type of battery, drawing on the established concepts of proton-exchange and anion-exchange membranes.The university says the quasi-solid membrane is non-flammable, potentially offering a safety advantage for energy storage applications. However, the study’s coin-cell tests do not establish the fire safety or commercial performance of a complete battery system.Fluoride-ion batteries could eventually find applications in stationary energy storage, electric vehicles and aviation. Their theoretical energy density could also exceed that of conventional lithium-ion technologies.The research team cited a potential energy density of around 600 watt-hours per kilogram, compared with approximately 150–250 Wh/kg for standard lithium-ion batteries. Such figures represent potential rather than performance demonstrated by the experimental cells.The work was coordinated by Maurizio Sansotera, with electrochemical characterization led by Luca Magagnin and molecular dynamics research contributed by Giuseppina Raffaini. Federico Maria Scesa was the paper’s lead author.Despite the progress, fluoride-ion batteries remain an emerging technology. Researchers still need to improve electrode materials, battery stability, cycle life, and overall performance before the chemistry can compete with established lithium-ion systems.The new membrane provides a possible route towards room-temperature fluoride-ion transport, bringing researchers a step closer to practical batteries that use a different charge carrier.The story appears in the journal Energy Storage Materials.

title: Can Claude dream now? Anthropic explores human-like machine memory
content: Science fiction has long imagined machines that think, learn, and perhaps even dream. Anthropic is now exploring an idea that sounds straight out of that world. Its latest research examines how Claude can revisit past experiences during periods of inactivity, correct faulty memories, and organize what it has learned for future conversations. Anthropic calls this process “dreaming,” although it has little to do with the dreams humans experience.The approach allows Claude to review previous interactions when it has idle time. It can identify incorrect information, refine existing notes, and build structured knowledge that future sessions can access. The process draws inspiration from how human brains consolidate memories during sleep.Anthropic’s research examines several components of this system. Its experiments suggest that selective memory and regular maintenance can improve performance on complex, long-running tasks.Teaching ClaudeClaude can save useful information in memory files while completing tasks. However, deciding what deserves storage presents a challenge. Recording every interaction creates clutter, while overlooking important details can leave future sessions without useful context.Anthropic tested this problem using Pokémon Red, where Claude had to navigate the game’s world and earn badges. The researchers compared two models after approximately 10,000 gameplay steps.Memory is what allows Claude to learn from experience. In a new Engineering Blog post, we share how “dreaming” helps Claude organize what it’s learned, correct its mistakes, and find what it needs more easily the next time. https://t.co/uUEN4bNkr9— Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) November 6, 2026Sonnet 3.7 recorded almost everything it encountered. Its memory directory contained 413 files across 225 folders, totaling nearly 978,000 characters. Despite maintaining this enormous record, the model earned just one badge.Claude Fable 5 took a considerably different approach. It maintained only 10 files across three locations, using approximately 43,400 characters. The model earned four badges during its run.The smaller memory system prioritized navigation strategies and lessons learned through gameplay. It also maintained a central file containing its current objectives and planned actions.This approach helped Claude avoid repeatedly processing information that it could already retrieve from the game’s interface. It also preserved useful discoveries that would otherwise disappear between sessions.Dreaming helps correct mistakesMemory files can contain incorrect information, creating problems when future sessions treat those details as established facts. Anthropic demonstrated how dreaming could address this issue through another Pokémon experiment.Claude incorrectly recorded the location of a Pokémon Center near Mt. Moon. The mistake caused it to misunderstand its position after leaving the building. It repeatedly walked over a one-way ledge and returned to an earlier route.An offline review changed the outcome. Claude compared its stored notes against the original session transcript and identified the incorrect location. It then updated the memory file with the correct information.With that correction, Claude re-entered Mt. Moon and eventually reached Cerulean City. The version using incorrect memory repeatedly encountered the same obstacle and never completed the journey.Building knowledge beyond conversationsAnthropic also explored whether dreaming could turn large document collections into interconnected knowledge bases. These systems resemble wikis, with individual pages linking related information.One experiment involved approximately 350,000 internal documents from software company Stainless. The collection contained roughly 420 million tokens.Across 128 sessions, Claude gradually developed and refined a wiki using information from those documents. Its performance on 25 evaluation questions improved from 13 percent to 48 percent.A separate merger-document experiment produced another notable result. Claude answered questions requiring information from multiple documents with 87 percent accuracy using its wiki. Direct document search alone achieved 73 percent.Dreaming can also reorganize information for future sessions. Claude can move frequently needed details into readily available context while keeping less relevant information in searchable files.Anthropic acknowledges that the approach still requires careful management. Memory maintenance consumes computing resources, and excessive information can overwhelm future sessions.The researchers believe agents must learn when to preserve information and when to revisit it. Their experiments suggest that better memory management could help Claude handle increasingly complicated tasks across multiple sessions.

title: IBM's Quantum System Two begins operations at Chicago research hub
content: IBM has brought its most advanced quantum computer to Chicago, giving researchers and businesses in Illinois access to the technology as the state builds a major hub for quantum research and development.The IBM Quantum System Two is now operational at Hyde Park Labs, where it is hosted by the University of Chicago. The system is powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, which the company describes as its most powerful quantum processor to date.Unveiled on November 6, the installation marks IBM’s first quantum computer deployment in Illinois. The machine will eventually move to the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park (IQMP), a technology campus currently under construction in Chicago.The computer will serve as the anchor system of the National Quantum Algorithm Center (NQAC), established in 2024 by Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, with IBM as a leading member. The center brings together companies, universities and research institutions to develop algorithms and applications that can scale with advances in quantum hardware.New system expands researchIBM said the system is intended to help organizations across Illinois explore computationally difficult problems using quantum computing.Among the projects already underway are efforts to develop quantum-based approaches to drug discovery. Deloitte and pharmaceutical company AbbVie are working with IBM and Northwestern University on molecular simulation methods through the NQAC Grand Challenges program.Another collaboration involves the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The partners are exploring whether quantum optimization algorithms could help make electricity grids more efficient.Fermilab is also working with IBM on high-energy physics research and technologies for distributed quantum computing.The University of Chicago and IBM have separately reported a demonstration of quantum advantage over leading classical methods using an approach with guaranteed correctness. The work highlights the research activity already taking place across the state’s quantum ecosystem.Chicago builds quantum hubThe arrival of System Two is part of a broader effort to position Illinois as a center for quantum technology and microelectronics. Once completed, IQMP will house research facilities and companies working to develop and commercialize technologies in these fields.IBM CEO Arvind Krishna said the deployment would help organizations across Illinois and beyond produce scientifically useful results. The company also expects the system to support the development of new algorithms and applications with potential real-world uses.The investment is also tied to workforce development. IBM previously announced plans to establish its FutureNow Chicago center at IQMP in partnership with City Colleges of Chicago. The initiative is expected to bring 750 jobs to the region across fields including quantum computing, cybersecurity and data science.Quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, to process information according to the principles of quantum mechanics. Unlike conventional bits, which represent either zero or one, qubits can exist in combinations of states. This enables quantum systems to tackle certain problems in ways that may be difficult for classical computers.However, practical applications remain an active area of research, and quantum machines are not replacements for conventional computers.For now, IBM’s Chicago deployment gives researchers and industry partners direct access to its latest quantum hardware as they work to identify problems where the technology can deliver an advantage.

title: 18-year-old quantum computing conjecture solved in just three days
content: An 18-year-old mathematical problem concerning the limits of quantum computing may finally have been solved in just three days. Physics research company PSI claims to have cracked the long-standing Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, potentially shedding new light on when quantum computers can outperform conventional machines.The company said its system completed the proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture in three days. The problem, first proposed in 2008, concerns the conditions under which quantum computers can achieve an exponential speed advantage over conventional computers.PSI said its research system used a non-public model from Anthropic, running on the company’s own infrastructure. The system produced a mathematical proof that was accepted by Lean, a proof-assistant software used to check the logical correctness of formal mathematical arguments.The company said the system subsequently improved the proof twice, with Lean accepting the final version as well.However, the result has not yet undergone full independent academic review. While researchers at Stanford University have examined aspects of the work and provided feedback, wider scrutiny will be important in establishing whether the proof resolves the original conjecture.A long-standing quantum questionThe Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture addresses how much information a classical computer needs to simulate certain quantum algorithms.More specifically, it concerns whether quantum algorithms with a particular mathematical structure can be efficiently approximated by classical computers. If the conjecture holds, classical computers could simulate a broad class of quantum algorithms on randomly selected inputs with only polynomial overhead. The distinction matters because polynomial and exponential growth can produce vastly different computing demands as the size of a problem increases.That would help explain why some quantum algorithms may not deliver an exponential advantage over classical computing, even if quantum hardware can process information in fundamentally different ways.The result does not mean quantum computers have no advantage over classical machines. Algorithms designed for particular problems, including Shor’s algorithm for factoring large numbers, are not ruled out by the conjecture.Instead, the conjecture addresses a specific class of quantum computations and the conditions under which their apparent advantage can be reproduced classically.Independent scrutiny remainsPSI said David Turturean led the work, developing the research system, defining the problem and running the process. He also reviewed the resulting draft and was responsible for the paper’s correctness.The company said Jim Halverson audited the proof, while Phiala Shanahan provided comments on its Lean formalisation.Researchers at Stanford, including Guy Blanc, Jordan Docter, Carmen Strassle and Li-Yang Tan, have also been examining the result. The group previously proved a special case of the conjecture in August 2026 and is preparing a shorter exposition of PSI’s full proof for other experts.Their involvement is significant because formal verification and independent mathematical review serve different purposes. Lean can check whether a formal proof follows logically from its stated assumptions, but researchers must also assess whether the formalized statement accurately captures the original conjecture.PSI, which launched publicly in September 2026, describes itself as a physics research company building automated systems for scientific discovery. Its announcement marks a potentially important milestone, but the claim will need to withstand broader expert review before it can be treated as a settled result.

title: SpaceX Falcon 9 launches secret payload for the US Space Force
content: SpaceX has completed another national security launch for the U.S. military, sending its Falcon 9 rocket into orbit with the classified USSF-432 payload. The mission lifted off from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California on November 7. Its first-stage booster subsequently returned to Earth and landed on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean.Designated USSF-432 and R-4, the mission adds another classified payload to the U.S. Space Force’s growing orbital operations. Officials have not disclosed the spacecraft’s identity, capabilities, or exact mission objectives. However, its suspected connection to a military satellite program offers some clues about the technology involved.Inside the classified missionUSSF-432 is part of a series of national security launches associated with the Space Force. Analysts have linked the R-series missions to the military’s Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio. The program aims to strengthen the military’s ability to gather information and support operations from orbit.The suspected payload could include satellites based on SpaceX’s Starshield platform. SpaceX developed Starshield specifically for government and national security customers. Its architecture draws on technology from the company’s commercial Starlink network. However, Starshield supports more specialized requirements, including secure communications and Earth observation.Liftoff! pic.twitter.com/v8mmRp00fG— SpaceX (@SpaceX) November 7, 2026Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force has confirmed the payload’s composition. Its satellite count and individual capabilities also remain undisclosed. Any connection to Starshield therefore remains an assessment rather than an established mission detail.Falcon 9 booster returnsThe launch marked the eighth flight for Falcon 9’s first-stage booster, identified as B1095. Its previous assignments included the GPS III-8 navigation satellite mission. The booster also supported six Starlink flights before taking on USSF-432.Falcon 9 separates its two stages during powered flight. The upper stage continues toward orbit with the payload. Meanwhile, the first stage begins its controlled return toward a designated recovery zone.Falcon 9’s first stage lands on the Of Course I Still Love You droneship pic.twitter.com/u5WQblzJlB— SpaceX (@SpaceX) November 7, 2026For this mission, B1095 targeted SpaceX’s Of Course I Still Love You droneship. The autonomous recovery vessel waited in the Pacific Ocean. After completing its descent sequence, the booster touched down on the platform.SpaceX can inspect and refurbish recovered boosters before assigning them to future missions. Reusing the first stage reduces the need to manufacture an entirely new booster for every launch. It also allows the company to maintain a high launch cadence.Starshield’s defense applicationsStarshield gives U.S. government customers access to satellite technology tailored to national security requirements. Its potential applications include secure data transmission and space-based observation. These capabilities can support military operations that depend on information gathered beyond Earth’s atmosphere.Space-based sensing and targeting systems can help military operators monitor activity across large geographic areas. They can also provide information that supports operational planning. However, the Space Force has not detailed how USSF-432 will contribute to these capabilities.The mission’s classified status leaves several technical questions unanswered. Its payload configuration and operational role remain unknown. Still, another successful launch gives the Space Force an additional mission in its expanding military satellite program.

title: SpaceX targets 2027 launch for orbital supercomputers with NVIDIA
content: Elon Musk is preparing to take high-performance computing beyond Earth’s atmosphere. SpaceX plans to begin launching its StarMind SI computing systems into orbit in the third quarter of 2027. The company expects deployment to accelerate through 2028 and 2029. He says the project could reshape how engineers approach large-scale computing infrastructure.Speaking with investor Ron Baron at the 33rd Annual Baron Investment Conference in New York, Musk teased more details about the project. “When we unveil the details of the StarMind computer next year, it will blow people’s minds,” he said.SpaceX is developing its first orbital computing systems alongside NVIDIA. The initial hardware will center on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 platform. The partnership brings advanced computing hardware into a project designed for operation beyond traditional terrestrial data centers.Supercomputing moves into orbitSpace-based computing could offer advantages beyond freeing data centers from land constraints. Musk also sees orbital infrastructure as an opportunity to rethink global data transmission.He discussed SpaceX’s upcoming Starlink Version 4 satellites during the interview. The next generation could deliver 10 times the capacity of Version 3. Musk said Version 3 already offers 10 times the capability of Version 2.When we unveil the details of the Starmind computer next year, it will blow people’s minds— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 6, 2026Laser communication will play a major role in that upgrade. SpaceX plans to equip each satellite with 10 next-generation laser links. Each link could deliver data transmission speeds exceeding 10 terabits per second.Musk also outlined a more ambitious possibility involving more than 100,000 satellites. He suggested that roughly 100 laser links per satellite could eventually challenge traditional undersea communications cables.His argument centers on transmission physics and network geometry. Light travels approximately 40% faster through space than through fiber-optic cables. Orbital connections can also follow more direct paths between distant destinations.Memphis becomes computing hubMusk also discussed SpaceX’s massive computing infrastructure project in Memphis, Tennessee. He described an unusually hands-on approach to developing the facility.The billionaire said he lives in an Airstream trailer beside its power plant. SpaceX built the facility’s power infrastructure in approximately one year. Elon Musk claimed the process typically takes around five years.The power plant now produces more than one gigawatt, according to the SpaceX chief. He also described personally handling electrical and networking work across the site.~100 lasers per satellite, each operating above 10 Tb/s, with over 100k satellites should be able to outcompete undersea cables. Speed of light in space is ~40% faster than cable and the path is direct, instead of following the outline of land masses. https://t.co/l7aqDUoTAK— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 6, 2026“I’ve pulled power cables the size of an anaconda,” Musk said. He added that he has worked on fiber-optic connections and network switches.Musk said he walks the facility up to five times daily. He wants direct exposure to the engineering challenges facing employees. His approach, he explained, helps him understand the difficulties workers encounter.He also defended the economic impact of large data centers. Musk argued that Memphis businesses have benefited from SpaceX’s presence. He cited stronger restaurant and hotel activity, higher wages, and additional local tax revenue.Tesla targets faster chip developmentThe interview also touched on Tesla’s expanding semiconductor ambitions. Musk revealed that Tesla is developing a research chip fabrication facility at Gigafactory Texas.The facility aims to shorten semiconductor development cycles dramatically. His target involves reducing processes that traditionally take approximately one year. He wants engineers to complete comparable development cycles in roughly one month.Tesla also plans to establish Terafab in Grimes County, Texas. The two facilities will serve different purposes. The Austin research operation will experiment with chip designs and manufacturing techniques. Terafab will focus on scaling successful developments into high-volume production.Tesla wants to bring multiple stages of semiconductor development under one roof. These include logic fabrication, memory production, lithography, and advanced packaging. The setup will also support chip testing.The broader ambition is to accelerate hardware development for Tesla’s growing computing requirements. However, Elon Musk’s orbital computing plans remain the central focus. SpaceX now has a 2027 launch target for its StarMind systems, with larger deployments expected afterward.

title: New hybrid amphibious aircraft unveiled, could carry 2,000-lb payload
content:
Hybrid amphibious aircraft integrates tremendous power of electric propulsion
“Our goal with the M1 Hybrid Cargo was to rethink what an amphibious aircraft can do,” said David Dillon, CEO of Maxwell Aircraft.
“By combining the tremendous power of electric
propulsion
where it delivers the greatest benefit with the range and energy density of Jet A for cruise, we saw we could give operators an aircraft that carries more, travels farther, and reaches destinations inaccessible to conventional landplanes. The M1-HC is designed to be a practical working aircraft—not just a technology demonstration.”
Hybrid amphibious aircraft has hybrid-drive architecture
At the heart of the M1 Hybrid Cargo is a mechanically coupled hybrid-drive architecture designed to match propulsion technology to each phase of flight. Conventional aircraft must carry engines sized for takeoff even though they use only a fraction of that power in cruise. Maxwell’s hybrid architecture is designed to overcome that compromise, combining short bursts of electric power with exceptionally efficient fuel-powered cruising,
according to
a press release.
Maxwell Aircraft revealed that the patent-pending mechanically coupled hybrid drive combines powerful electric motors with high-efficiency compression-ignition engines with design targets of up to 1,500 horsepower for takeoff and initial climb and approximately 300 horsepower combined during cruise (150 horsepower per engine). Limiting electric boost primarily to these high-power phases reduces the amount of battery capacity—and battery weight—the aircraft must carry.
During cruise, the M1 relies on high-efficiency, compound-turbocharged, direct-injection compression-ignition engines operating on widely available Jet A fuel. The combination is designed to provide the energy density required for long-range operations while retaining the performance advantages of electric propulsion, as per the release.
Maxwell also highlighted that the aircraft is being designed around the practical requirements of cargo and logistics operators. A five-foot cargo door enables efficient loading and unloading of palletized freight, while the amphibious configuration provides access to both unimproved runways and waterways.
This flexibility could make the M1 Hybrid Cargo particularly well suited for missions involving remote communities, island operations, logistics, disaster response, government agencies, and defense organizations. The M1 Hybrid Cargo is available under experimental aircraft regulations, including commercial use for government purposes. Other applications include government operations and defense missions worldwide, as per the release.

title: US starts production of key material used in nuclear weapons
content: The United States has restored its significant nuclear weapons manufacturing capability. The country has recently produced a specialized material used in U.S. nuclear weapons for the first time in 20 years. “Under the Trump Administration, NNSA is making sweeping investments to revitalize the nation’s nuclear weapons infrastructure,” said NNSA Administrator Brandon Williams. “This is not just about a warhead ingredient. This shift symbolizes our commitment to the long-term health of our weapons stockpile and the lasting security of our country.”Production of a key nuclear material known as ‘binary’ alloyThe National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) has qualified the Y-12 National Security Complex to resume production of a material known as “binary” alloy, ending two decades of reliance on a limited supply of material manufactured years ago.Nuclear material binary alloy is used to manufacture radiation casesBinary alloy is used to manufacture radiation cases, which enclose essential components within America’s nuclear weapons. Restoring the ability to produce this material gives the United States a renewed source for maintaining and modernizing its nuclear stockpile, according to a press release. Experts from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and Los Alamos National Laboratory evaluated both the manufacturing process and the finished materials before NNSA granted approval to resume production. Y-12 is also working to improve practices to use weapon materials more efficiently, ensuring that adequate supplies will be available for future stockpile needs, while still meeting all Department of War warhead requirements, as per the release. Binary alloy production has implications beyond manufacturing sectorThe restoration of binary alloy production has implications beyond the manufacturing sector. It is also connected to the broader strategic priorities of the United States.The U.S. considers the reliability and sustainability of its nuclear deterrent an important component of national security. A dependable domestic supply chain for critical nuclear weapons materials can help reduce vulnerabilities associated with ageing inventories and production interruptions.The development comes at a time when nuclear deterrence, strategic competition and the modernisation of military capabilities remain important issues in international security.For the U.S., restoring this capability strengthens an important part of its nuclear weapons industrial base. Nevertheless, the development should be understood as an infrastructure and manufacturing milestone rather than evidence of an expansion in the number of nuclear weapons.For nearly two decades, the U.S. relied on a limited existing supply of binary alloy. While this stockpile supported its requirements during that period, the restoration of production provides a more sustainable basis for meeting future needs. It also reflects a broader challenge facing nuclear-armed countries: maintaining ageing nuclear arsenals while ensuring that the industrial capabilities required to support them remain functional. The U.S. is seeking to address this challenge through investments in manufacturing facilities, technical expertise and the modernisation of its nuclear security infrastructure. The Y-12 facility is also working to improve material-use practices to ensure that available resources are utilised more efficiently while meeting the requirements of the country’s nuclear weapons programme.

title: Google DeepMind finds 1,600x faster way to expose encryption flaws
content: Google DeepMind researchers have used AI agents to discover cryptographic techniques that expose weaknesses in legacy RSA encryption up to 1,600 times faster than previous methods.​This breakthrough was announced by DeepMind’s Vice President and Chief Scientist, Pushmeet Kohli, in a social media post today.​The research marks a significant advance in the field of cryptanalysis while leaving modern encryption standards unaffected.No threat to modern encryption​The research focused on 1024-bit RSA, an outdated encryption standard largely replaced by stronger 2048-bit or larger keys. According to Google DeepMind, the findings do not threaten modern encryption used to secure online banking, messaging apps, software updates, or digital currencies. Instead, they show how AI can dramatically accelerate the evaluation of the mathematical assumptions that underpin digital security.​Cryptanalysis is the science of testing encryption systems by searching for weaknesses before malicious actors can exploit them. For decades, advances in the field have typically taken years or even decades, allowing security experts to gradually strengthen encryption standards as computing capabilities evolved.​The company said its AI agents, working under human supervision, compressed that timeline by rapidly exploring mathematical problems that traditionally required extensive manual research.​The study, led by Dj Dvijotham and Abhradeep Thakurta in collaboration with researchers from the University of California San Diego and France’s Inria, produced two major findings involving legacy RSA-1024 cryptosystems.“Padding” prevents forgery​The first concerns digital signatures, which allow computers to verify that software updates, websites, and electronic documents come from legitimate sources.​Digital signature schemes typically add extra preset information, known as “padding,” before signing data. Padding has long been understood to prevent forgery, but researchers had not fully quantified its effectiveness when attackers can influence portions of the signed message.​During the research, the AI agents found that once an attacker controls roughly half of the signed data block or more, padding offers virtually no additional protection. Under those conditions, forging a digital signature becomes mathematically no more difficult than attacking an unpadded system.​To validate the discovery, the researchers tested the method in a sandbox environment using an already-solved RSA-1024 benchmark from earlier academic work. The AI-generated implementation reproduced the result while requiring 3.5 times less CPU time and less than one-thousandth of the computational power needed to factor the benchmark key itself.​Even when attackers control only a small portion of the signed data, such as a 32-byte digital fingerprint, the AI agents identified a new algorithm that theoretically improves upon the previous best attack by approximately 1,600 times for 1024-bit RSA keys.AI reduces computational cost of cryptanalysisThe second breakthrough targets the batch factorization of multiple RSA keys with the same bit length. Since many RSA deployments use standardized key sizes, attackers could theoretically share the cost of expensive computations across numerous keys.​The AI-discovered algorithm improves the asymptotic efficiency of that process, reducing the average computational cost of factoring each additional 1024-bit RSA key by about 30 times compared with previous batch techniques.​Kohli said the results reinforce the need to continuously reassess cryptographic assumptions as AI becomes increasingly capable of tackling advanced mathematical problems.​While today’s encryption standards remain secure, the researchers argue that AI-powered cryptanalysis could become an essential tool for stress-testing future cryptographic systems before emerging threats put them at risk.

title: Goodbye, Cybertruck? Tesla plans to wind down production in 2027
content: Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory around mid-2027 to make room for increased production of its Cybercab robotaxi, marking a major shift in the electric vehicle maker’s manufacturing priorities.CEO Elon Musk announced the move in a post on X on Friday, saying the company would redirect factory capacity towards the two-seat autonomous vehicle. He did not clarify whether Cybertruck production would move to another facility or end altogether. The decision comes after the stainless-steel electric pickup struggled to achieve the sales volumes Tesla had initially anticipated. It also underscores Musk’s growing focus on autonomous transportation as the company looks beyond conventional electric vehicles.The Cybertruck was unveiled in 2019 with an angular stainless-steel exterior that set it apart from traditional pickups. Tesla initially planned to begin production in 2021 but faced several delays before delivering the first customer vehicles in November 2023.Cybertruck sales stuck in slow laneMusk had previously projected annual Cybertruck sales of up to 250,000 units. However, the pickup has struggled to attract buyers beyond its niche following, with its unconventional design, high price and production issues limiting its commercial reach.According to Cox Automotive estimates, Tesla sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US in 2025, down 48% from 38,965 units in 2024. The figures highlight the gap between the company’s original ambitions and actual demand. The vehicle has also faced multiple recalls and quality-control problems since its launch. These included issues involving its accelerator pedal, exterior components, and drive systems, adding to the challenges surrounding its production and ownership.Tesla does not separately disclose Cybertruck sales in its quarterly delivery reports, making it difficult to assess the model’s performance using the company’s own figures.The production wind-down does not necessarily mean Tesla is abandoning the pickup altogether. Musk later responded to a post describing the decision as the end of an era, saying the existing Cybertruck fleet would remain around for a long time, without providing details about future production plans. Cybercab takes production priorityThe factory space freed up by the move will support increased production of the Cybercab, Tesla’s purpose-built autonomous electric vehicle designed for its robotaxi network.Unveiled in October 2024, the Cybercab has two passenger seats and does away with conventional driving controls, including a steering wheel and pedals. Tesla envisions the vehicle operating without a human driver as part of an autonomous ride-hailing service.The company has already started production of the Cybercab, according to its second-quarter 2026 update, and has been testing production vehicles on public roads. However, scaling up the robotaxi program will depend on Tesla’s ability to expand its autonomous driving operations and meet regulatory requirements. Driverless vehicle deployment remains subject to safety oversight, while the company has yet to demonstrate that its robotaxi model can operate at scale across multiple markets.The shift also reflects a broader change in Tesla’s ambitions. Musk has increasingly positioned robotics and autonomous transportation as central to the company’s future, alongside its electric vehicle and energy businesses.By redirecting factory capacity from the Cybertruck to the Cybercab, Tesla is making a clear manufacturing bet on that strategy. Whether the robotaxi can deliver the commercial success that eluded its electric pickup remains to be seen.
