title: 'Message to the West': Bomb threats target European flights, newsrooms
content: European newsrooms received chilling bomb threats warning that “the clock is ticking” on Friday, prompting evacuations and broadcast suspensions across the continent. The messages threatened imminent explosions and claimed responsibility for a wider campaign targeting passenger aircraft across Europe.Ireland’s public broadcaster RTÉ evacuated its offices after receiving an email warning that an explosive device would detonate within 45 minutes. Bulgaria’s Nova TV received a similar message, while Britain’s Sky also reported a security threat.No explosives have been discovered at any affected location. Investigators have not established whether the newsroom threats share a source with the growing wave of aviation disruptions.Emails Threaten Imminent ExplosionsThe emails sent to RTÉ and Nova TV carried the subject line “Message to the West.” They were signed by someone identifying himself as Mikhail Andropov, who claimed to lead a group behind the recent aviation threats.One message warned that an operative had planted an explosive device inside a broadcaster’s building. It gave authorities just 45 minutes before the alleged detonation.“But this is only the beginning. What happened this week is just a small part of what awaits Europe in the near future,” the sender wrote.RTÉ suspended programming and evacuated its offices while security teams investigated. Some broadcasts disappeared for as long as three hours, replaced by music and prerecorded announcements.Police inspected Nova TV’s newsroom in Sofia and declared the building safe. Employees subsequently returned to their desks, and the broadcaster maintained its programming.Sky also confirmed receiving a security threat. However, authorities have not disclosed whether its warning contained similar language or originated from the same sender.Aviation Threats Disrupt FlightsThe newsroom warnings followed several days of bomb threats targeting European aviation. The first major wave emerged Tuesday, affecting at least seven flights and a cruise ship.Threats prompted emergency landings, flight diversions and fighter jet escorts across Poland, Bulgaria, Italy and Spain. Another wave struck Thursday, affecting at least 27 flights.Friday brought further disruption across the continent. Prague’s Vaclav Havel Airport reported nine threatened flights, including services connecting Denmark, Spain and Britain.France also reported threats against at least four flights. A Ryanair service scheduled to travel from Lisbon to Rome encountered another alert.At least three aircraft received escorts from Hungarian fighter jets during Friday’s incidents. Every affected aircraft landed safely, and authorities have found no explosives aboard the threatened planes.Investigators probe threat campaignAuthorities have yet to identify the person behind the newsroom emails or establish whether all the threats share a common source. Investigators are examining the messages alongside the wider wave of aviation disruptions.The incidents have exposed how anonymous bomb threats can disrupt critical infrastructure without any confirmed explosives. Each alert forces security teams to investigate potential dangers before normal operations can resume.Aviation security specialist Eric Schouten told Reuters that airline security departments initially assess incoming threats through established procedures. They then alert authorities, who can order flight diversions or deploy fighter aircraft when necessary.Recent cyberattacks targeting supermarket refrigeration systems have also heightened security concerns across Europe. Investigators have not established any connection between those incidents and the bomb threats.No explosives have been discovered at the affected aircraft or broadcasting facilities. However, the sender’s warning that this is only the beginning has left European authorities facing the possibility of further disruptions.

title: US ally's startup enters NATO framework, boosts counter-drone availability
content: A French startup, Alta Ares, entered the North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s (NATO) counter-drone framework agreement.​The development, revealed on November 5, allows the allied partner countries to procure protective systems against aerial threats directly from the French defense manufacturer without the need for new tenders.​The company secured 16 awarded lots under the contract, bagging the highest number of awards among the five companies covered under the NATO procurement catalog. Northrop Grumman and Axon Enterprise from the United States, Quantum Systems from Germany, and OSL from the United Kingdom are the other four parties to the latest agreement of the international military alliance.Faster procurement of listed items​Expanding on the Framework Contract for Counter-Unmanned Aircraft Systems (C-UAS), which is a part of Drone Edge Marketplace under NATO’s Rapid Adoption Action Plan, the company said it has been designed to shorten procurement cycles through a catalog of preselected systems, allowing the allied countries to buy or lease the defense system.​”This new procurement model gives Allies speed and agility against rapidly evolving threats,” the company said.​Without sharing many details about the specifics of the weapon system, the company said that the six lots cover area defense and border protection. “It is the only supplier selected for area defense across all three mobility levels: static, transportable, and on-the-move,” the company said in a statement.​The said category spans different military requirements, which include protecting munition depots and air bases, and could expand to deploying temporary defensive positions or assisting military units near the conflict areas.Battle-tested “kill systems”​The French company highlighted that its “kill systems” are battle-tested, with its software drawing on the operational data collected in Ukraine and the Gulf.​”Its systems are built against the threat, not just tested against it,” it said.​The company has deployed its counter-drone technologies in Ukraine since 2024, where it has received direct feedback from deployed units operating against aerial threats such as Shahed-type one-way attack drones and loitering munitions.​”A counter-drone system has to work end-to-end, from detecting a threat to intercepting it. We built Alta Ares around that requirement, with software informed by battlefield data from Ukraine,” said Hadrien Canter, CEO and founder of Alta Ares.​The interceptor technologies developed by the company include Pixel Lock, a computer-vision solution designed for target detection and tracking, and Cyclop C2, which supports interceptor guidance using information provided by connected sensors and command systems. The other interceptor weapon system built by the French startup is the X-Lock interceptor with a stated range of over 9 miles (15 kilometers) and a maximum speed of nearly 200 miles per hour (310 km/hr). Black Bird, a turbojet-powered interceptor project, doubles the announced speed, 435 mph (700 km/hr), and range, 19 miles (30 km), of the X-Lock interceptor, is also part of the company’s ammunition against the growing drone threats in modern warfare.​The company has not mentioned which of these configurations made it to the NATO framework.​However, following the selection, the company is boosting production with its industrial partners and establishing dedicated teams to support contract implementation.​”We are committed to making affordable, next-generation air defense capabilities available at the scale Allied countries need,” Canter added.​For larger orders, the company is considering production arrangements in customer countries while expanding its European supply chain.

title: Drone-killing Citadel system with radar, 30mm cannon gets wheels
content: Russia’s Rostec has developed a mobile version of its Citadel air defense artillery system, moving the weapon and its detection equipment from a stationary installation onto a vehicle chassis. The change is intended to let Russian air defense teams relocate the system more quickly to sites requiring protection against drones and other aerial threats.Rostec announced the development on November 6, saying the new configuration places the combat module, radar and optical detection systems on a vehicle. The corporation did not disclose the chassis type, vehicle specifications, deployment timeline, or whether the mobile version has entered production.The original Citadel was designed to protect stationary facilities. Rostec says it has demonstrated effectiveness in combat against different types of drones and cruise missiles, although the company has not published independently verified performance data.How the Citadel system detects and engages dronesCitadel, also identified as the ZAK-30, is a 30 mm anti-aircraft artillery system. Rather than relying on guided missiles, it uses automatic guns and specialized ammunition intended to destroy aerial targets at relatively short ranges.The system combines radar with electro-optical sensors to detect and track incoming threats. Rostec says its optical equipment operates in both visible and infrared wavelengths, allowing it to track targets in different lighting conditions.Its ammunition is another defining feature. Citadel uses shrapnel-filled projectiles with remotely controlled fuses. Instead of relying entirely on a direct hit, the fire-control system calculates an appropriate detonation point based on the target’s flight path. The projectile then releases fragments near the aircraft, creating a cloud that can damage or destroy it.This approach is particularly relevant against small drones, which can be difficult to hit with conventional gunfire because of their size and maneuverability. Programmable airburst ammunition can increase the likelihood of hitting a target without requiring a projectile to strike it directly. Rostec also claims that fewer rounds are needed per engagement compared with conventional ammunition.Why put the system on a vehicle?The move to a vehicle-mounted configuration addresses a limitation of the original design: a stationary air defense installation is tied to the location it protects.Mounting Citadel on a vehicle could allow operators to move the system between airfields, industrial facilities, military sites, and other locations as threats change. It could also make it easier to reinforce areas facing increased drone activity without building a new permanent installation at each site.Mobility is particularly important for short-range air defense, which often provides the final layer of protection around valuable infrastructure and military assets. Such systems are intended to engage threats that penetrate wider air defense networks, including low-flying drones and cruise missiles.The Center for Strategic and International Studies describes Russian air defense as a layered structure, with short-range systems such as Pantsir providing point defense for important locations. Citadel’s role appears to fit within this broader category of close-range protection rather than replacing longer-range missile systems.A shift toward gun-based counter-drone defensesCitadel is part of a trend toward using automatic cannons and programmable ammunition against drones. One comparable system is Germany’s Rheinmetall Skynex, which uses 35 mm guns and programmable AHEAD ammunition to provide short-range air defense.Like Citadel, the German modular air defense system Skynex combines sensors, target tracking and gun-based engagement. Rheinmetall says its system is particularly suited to very short-range situations where guided missiles may be less practical or more expensive. Its architecture can also connect different sensors and weapons through a command-and-control network.The comparison shows why gun-based systems are receiving renewed attention. Using a relatively inexpensive projectile against a low-cost drone can help avoid expending more expensive guided missiles on every target. However, gun systems have limited engagement ranges and require accurate detection and tracking, making them one component of a layered defense rather than a complete solution. The mobile Citadel configuration adds flexibility to a system originally intended to guard fixed facilities.

title: European scientists spot new quantum state of matter at room temperature
content: A collaborative effort from researchers across various institutes in Europe has led to the observation of a new quantum state of matter called a supersolid in an exciton-polariton Bose-Einstein condensate. The quantum state is electrically tunable and is seen at room temperature, paving the way for quantum photonic devices in the future. As early as the 1960s, physicists theorized that a superfluid could develop in a crystal-like structure. A superfluid is an extraordinary state of matter where viscosity is completely lost and the fluid can move through narrow channels without any resistance. That it can exist in a rigid structure of a crystal seems contradictory. Yet in 2017, the resultant phase of their coexistence, called supersolid, was experimentally observed in ultracold atomic Bose-Einstein condensates. A team of researchers from the University of Warsaw, the Military University of Technology (Poland), IBM Research Zurich, and the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS) took the other route to see if such a quantum state could be reached at room temperature. Quantum state using lightIn their approach, the researchers used strong coupling between light and matter inside an optical microcavity to generate exciton polaritons – hybrid quasiparticles. The optical microcavity was filled with a specially designed liquid crystal and coated with an organic semiconductor, which enabled coupling even at room temperature. While these quasiparticles last for only a few picoseconds, it is long enough to form a Bose-Einstein condensate that then behaves like a quantum superfluid. When this superfluid transitions into a supersolid is known by observing regularly spaced bright fringes of light emitted from the sample. Interestingly, though, every laser pulse used to excite the sample generated bright fringes at different positions. ““This is a textbook example of spontaneous symmetry breaking,” explained Guillaume Malpuech, a professor at the Institut Pascal (CNRS). “Theory predicted that the supersolid could choose among several equivalent states, and that is exactly what we observed.”The team also observed two distinct forms of order simultaneously: one in polarization, the other in light intensity. Challenging researchSince the organic semiconductor reacted with the liquid crystal, the researchers needed to ensure that all measurements were completed within a few hours of the sample being assembled. Repeating an experiment would mean starting off with a new sample, making the research more challenging than anticipated. IBM Research Zurich was tasked with making the measurements and depositing thin films of organic semiconductors on the photonic structures made by Military University of Technology. While IBM Research Zurich has worked with organic semiconductor films for years and even observed Bose-Einstein condensates in them, this is the first time they have worked with a liquid-crystal microcavity, the press release said. Most studies of exotic quantum states require ultracold temperatures hovering near absolute zero. This study, however, shows that using photonic systems, such quantum states can also be observed at room temperature. “Our liquid-crystal microcavities can operate even at temperatures approaching 60°C,” added Wiktor Piecek, a professor at the Military University of Technology. Because optical microcavities can be tuned and their properties changed with an external voltage, they enable more practical quantum photonic devices and can also help study quantum phases of light and matter. The research findings were published in Science Advances.

title: NASA’s Moon capsule production accelerates ahead of Artemis missions
content: As NASA tightens its timeline to establish a permanent human outpost on the Moon, primary contractor Lockheed Martin is accelerating its manufacturing philosophy. The defense giant is turning the production of the Orion spacecraft into a streamlined assembly line designed to support NASA’s upcoming Artemis III, IV, and V missions.Overall, these efforts will support NASA’s revamped Artemis framework and Ignition directives designed to establish a sustained human presence on the Moon. Technicians analyze the heat shield tiles for the Orion Artemis IV spacecraft. Speeding up Orion productionThe Orion spacecraft is being designed to survive deep space while prioritizing human safety and high-rate manufacturing. Its life support system maintains a breathable environment for four crew members during extended flights. For atmospheric re-entry, the capsule features a 16.5-foot Avcoat heat shield built to withstand 5,000°F heat at speeds approaching 25,000 mph. Spacecraft operations utilize multi-redundant computers, data networks, and glass cockpit displays to allow automated monitoring and manual control. Transitioning from a “development mindset” to a “production mindset” requires changing how space hardware gets certified.Lockheed Martin experts and engineers are using data from previous flights to skip repetitive qualification testing, rather than treating every Orion capsule as an unproven prototype. Once a design is proven flightworthy, testing focuses exclusively on verifying build quality.“Once a design is qualified, acceptance testing can focus on verifying that each unit was built correctly,” said Tim Norick, Lockheed Martin Orion program hardware director. “We’re using experience from previous flights to reduce testing time and scope while preserving the must-do tests and evidence needed to confirm flight readiness and protect crew safety.”Lockheed Martin is also reusing flight-qualified hardware from prior Artemis missions to cut costs and protect flight schedules. Lockheed Martin has expanded its Orion workforce by adding over 100 technicians and support personnel, pushing operations to a round-the-clock, three-shift schedule, seven days a week.“Acceleration comes down to three things: putting more resources against the work, doing the work more efficiently, and reducing unnecessary scope and avoidable rework,” said Scott Daniels, Orion Assembly, Integration, and Test director at Kennedy.To the moon and beyond To keep assembly lines moving, the program introduced dedicated “Rapid Response Teams.” When an unexpected technical anomaly pops up on the floor, these senior subject matter experts jump in to resolve it immediately.“We’re embedding authority within various levels so the right people can react quickly when a problem arises, rather than losing time in a long chain of decisions,” said Brian Hinde, Lockheed Martin Orion Production Engineering senior manager. This approach keeps core integration crews focused on meeting primary delivery targets without getting bogged down by administrative delays.Accelerated production goals reach far down into the supply chain. Infrastructure upgrades at NASA’s Michoud Assembly Facility in Louisiana boosted the manufacturing of Orion’s Avcoat heat shield. Facility expansions and improved tooling increased weekly output from roughly four material billets to more than 20.Artemis I completed an uncrewed flight around the Moon, and Artemis II subsequently carried four astronauts on a historic lunar flyby. Artemis III will follow as a crewed orbital rendezvous test in Earth orbit, laying the essential technical groundwork for Artemis IV to execute the first crewed lunar surface landing since Apollo 17. This progression would help transition from temporary visits to a permanent human outpost on the Moon, using lessons learned on the lunar surface as a stepping stone for eventual crewed missions to Mars.

title: AQUILA interceptor uses 3-stage design for hypersonic aerial threats
content: At the Euronaval 2026 defense exhibition, European missile consortium MBDA reportedly provided design details for AQUILA. It is an endo-atmospheric interceptor built to dismantle both hypersonic weapons and medium-range ballistic missiles in one fell swoop.The AQUILA interceptor will use a 3-stage architecture comprising a booster accelerator, cruiser, and kill-vehicle to perform long-range, high-altitude engagements against high-velocity maneuvering threats.AQUILA forms the technological core of the European Hypersonic Defense Interceptor Study (HYDIS). The program is locked in a high-stakes competition against the rival HYDEF project to secure the continent’s next-generation shield against emerging aerial threats. “AQUILA is MBDA’s first interceptor concept specifically designed to counter hypersonic threats. It embodies a new generation of endo-atmospheric defense, reinforcing MBDA’s air-defense portfolio and ensuring more durable and effective protection of high-value assets and deployed forces in an increasingly contested environment,” the company noted.AQUILA. CREDIT: MBDAAmbitious AQUILA hypersonic interceptorThe rapid evolution of hypersonic systems over the past decade has created a major strategic challenge. Extreme speeds and unpredictable flight trajectories make maneuvering ballistic missiles, hypersonic cruise missiles, and hypersonic glide vehicles exceptionally difficult to counter. MBDA addressed this gap by investing heavily in research and development to create AQUILA, an advanced endo-atmospheric interceptor for modern atmospheric defense. An endo-atmospheric interceptor is a defense missile built to detect, track, and eliminate airborne threats within Earth’s atmosphere.MBDA officially unveiled the AQUILA concept to the public at the Paris Air Show (Le Bourget) in 2023.What makes AQUILA a standout? It attempts what no current Western defense platform can.Prompted by the combat emergence of maneuvering threats like Russia’s Kinzhal and Zircon missiles, European military planners realized traditional air defenses were falling behind. The Pentagon currently splits this massive operational burden across multiple dedicated platforms. It relies on the SM-3 and THAAD for ballistic missile defense and is developing the Glide Phase Interceptor (GPI) for maneuvering hypersonic glide vehicles.Europe wants a single effector to handle the entire spectrum. To pull off this feat, MBDA finalized a 3-stage, all-rocket configuration.The interceptor features four all-rocket-propelled stages, a design choice settled upon to deliver extreme acceleration. Speed matters. The missile will execute direct “hit-to-kill” engagements across vastly different altitudes. At the edge of the atmosphere, AQUILA will target Intermediate-Range Ballistic Missiles (IRBMs) with ranges up to 3,000 kilometers (1,864 miles). Lower down, it will hunt elusive Hypersonic Glide Vehicles (HGVs) and hypersonic cruise missiles.Stronger air defense for EuropeSize constraints are equally critical.AQUILA is designed for easy naval integration, built to fit standard Mk-41 Vertical Launch Systems (VLS) and upgraded SYLVER naval launchers. Operationally, a battery can protect a 100-kilometer zone using only its organic radar system. Even so, network feeds from space sensors and radar grids will dramatically boost its target acquisition.Engineered for both land and ship platforms, the system complements the proven ASTER missile family, reinforcing integrated air and missile defense architectures to neutralize emerging hypersonic threats.If successful, MBDA’s four-stage bet will streamline Europe’s air defenses.

title: Counter-drone air defense system fires 3,000 rounds per minute in trial
content:
Designed to protect military convoys
ASGARD has been developed as a medium-weight, remotely operated air defense turret designed to protect military convoys, ground forces and critical infrastructure against low-flying aerial threats.
The system has a reported combat weight of approximately 1,850-lb and 2,094-lb and provides full 360-degree traverse capability. Its elevation range extends from -10 to +80 degrees, while its maximum angular movement speed is stated to reach 120 degrees per second.
The primary weapon tested during the recent trials was the Dillon Aero M134D, a six-barrel, electrically driven Gatling gun chambered for 7.62×51 mm NATO ammunition.
The effectiveness of a Gatling gun against small UAVs depends on more than its firing rate. Target detection, tracking accuracy, sensor integration and fire-control capabilities are equally important.
ASGARD fires 3,000 rounds/min
The weapon has a firing rate of 3,000 rounds per minute, equivalent to approximately 50 rounds per second. Its multi-barrel design distributes firing cycles across six barrels, supporting sustained firing while distributing heat and mechanical stress.
Gun-based counter-drone systems offer another layer of defense, potentially providing a more economical option against certain categories of short-range aerial threats.
ASGARD’s remotely operated configuration is intended to support integration onto military vehicles, allowing it to accompany ground formations rather than remain restricted to fixed
defensive
positions. The ASGARD program also reflects Slovenia’s broader efforts to strengthen its domestic defense industrial
capabilities
ASGARD represents an attempt to combine a modular remotely operated turret with an established high-rate-of-fire weapon system.
Its ultimate operational value will depend on the performance of the complete system rather than the Gatling gun alone. Reliable detection, identification, tracking and fire-control integration will be essential in determining whether it can provide effective protection under realistic battlefield conditions.

title: 3632°F heat turns old wind turbine blades to silicon carbide, graphene
content: Researchers at Tsinghua University have developed an “upcycling” method using flash Joule heating to turn retired wind turbine blades into silicon carbide and graphene. These two are high-value materials used in manufacturing.Giant wind turbine blades are designed to survive the unthinkable. They slice through freezing gales, endure relentless UV radiation, and withstand lightning strikes for over two decades. But that extreme durability turns into an environmental issue when their service life ends. Decommissioned blades mostly end up buried in landfills.China-based team has now unlocked a solution to this long-standing dilemma. The chemical and environmental engineers found a way to transform tough composite waste into high-value manufacturing materials using a brief burst of extreme heat.Researchers prepared resin samples reinforced with silicon carbide and graphene recovered from discarded wind turbine blades for a tensile performance test. Credit: Hao Bi.A thermal miracle in secondsThe wind power surge of the early 2000s has created an urgent disposal crisis today as the first major generation of 20-year turbine blades reaches retirement. Annual decommissioned blade waste across China, Europe, and the U.S. now reaches thousands of tons. Outright landfill bans on composite waste in nations like Germany and Austria make finding scalable alternative processing methods an imperative for the renewable energy sector.“As aging turbines are decommissioned, especially in China, where wind power has expanded rapidly, much of the waste has ended up in landfills. It’s a waste of resources,” said Bing Deng, senior author and chemical and environmental engineer at Tsinghua University, China. The key was found in the raw ingredients already inside every blade. Turbine blades are built from silica-rich fiberglass bound together by carbon-dense resin.In this new work, researchers used flash Joule heating to zap broken blade material to roughly 2,000°C (3,632°F) in a matter of seconds.The intense heat triggers a rapid reaction in which carbon bonds with silica to form silicon carbide, a ultra-hard, heat-tolerant compound. At the same time, the remaining carbon atoms restructure into graphene, one of the strongest and most conductive nanomaterials known to science.Integrating tiny amounts of the recovered silicon carbide and graphene mixture directly into fresh resin boosted performance. A 0.3 percent weight addition strengthens the resin, increasing tensile deformation resistance by 27 percent and flexural strength by 9 percent. Adding a mere 0.1 percent concentration boosts thermal diffusivity by 41 percent, allowing heat to disperse far more efficiently.This upgraded material can be used to construct next-generation wind turbine blades, creating a closed-loop system where old turbines help build stronger new ones.Upcycling with a profit marginExisting recycling methods like pyrolysis and solvent dissolution carry heavy price tags and high carbon footprints. Flash Joule heating could also change the economic model. “With conventional recycling methods, you have to spend money to process the waste. But our method could actually turn a profit of about $80 per ton because the recovered silicon carbide and graphene are valuable,” said lead author and environmental engineer Hao Bi of Tsinghua University. “By comparison, pyrolysis costs about $460 per ton, while chemical dissolution costs about $1,800 per ton.” The team is currently scaling up the process for industrial deployment. Broadening the technology could also help upcycle composite materials from aerospace, automotive, and electronics industries.The team published the findings in the journal Chem Circularity.

title: Scientists Find That Older Brains React Very Differently to a Night of Poor Sleep
content:
A new study reveals that younger and older brains respond in surprisingly different ways to a single night of sleep deprivation. Credit: Shutterstock
A single bad night’s sleep may be easier on a healthy older brain than a younger one, though regularly missing sleep still carries risks.
Sleep quality often declines with age, yet older adults can seem less affected by a single bad night than younger people. Understanding that apparent mismatch means looking at how the brain responds when sleep runs short.
A study from
Simon Fraser University
offers a possible explanation. After just three hours of sleep, certain connections in younger and older brains changed in opposite directions. The findings suggest that healthy older brains may adapt to acute sleep loss in ways that help preserve function, although the study measured brain activity rather than cognitive performance.
The research, published in
Imaging Neuroscience
, compared brain networks in younger adults ages 20 to 30 with those in older adults ages 65 to 75. Lead researcher Josh Neudorf, an affiliate member of SFU’s Institute for Neuroscience and Neurotechnology, says earlier research on the effects of poor sleep provided a reason to investigate the difference.
“Older adults tend to better handle the effects of poor sleep, whereas younger adults, as we know, have the common symptoms of decreased mood and cognitive ability following poor sleep,” says Neudorf.
“This study tries to get at the heart of this difference – how does the older brain react to lost sleep.”
How brain networks handle a short night
Brain connectivity describes how activity in different regions is linked. Stronger connections do not automatically mean the brain is working more efficiently. The arrangement matters, too. In a more modular network, regions are organized into groups, with relatively stronger connections within each group than between groups.
“What we found was quite striking in that older and younger brains actually responded in opposite ways to acute sleep loss.
“Certain connections in the brains of younger adults showed increased connectivity as a response to less sleep, while those same connections in the brains of older adults showed decreased connectivity.
“That decrease in connectivity promotes more efficient modular connectivity for the brain as a whole. In other words, the brain is acting in a more efficient way to maintain cognitive function. In contrast, the increased connectivity in younger brains suggests the brain is having to work harder to maintain function.”
Whether those network changes actually helped the older participants think or perform tasks better was not tested. The proposed benefit is an interpretation of the brain activity, consistent with previous research suggesting that older adults are often less impaired by a single night of poor sleep.
The reason for the opposite responses also remains open. One of several possible explanations is compensation, in which an aging brain reorganizes its networks and uses different strategies to maintain function.
“The quality of sleep starts to change and deteriorates somewhat in older adults,” says Neudorf.
“The theory of compensation is the idea that older brains adapt or compensate for those changes.”
Chronic sleep loss still harms health
Being able to adjust to an occasional short night would not make regularly missing sleep harmless. Researchers emphasize that good-quality sleep matters throughout life. Although the response to one or two nights of lost sleep may differ with age, chronic sleep loss is detrimental to brain health and cognitive ability. Its cumulative effects over a lifetime also have the potential to increase the risk of cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, weight problems, and colorectal cancer.
Dementia presents another concern. Study co-author Brianne Kent is an assistant professor of psychology, associate director of SFU’s Institute for Neuroscience and Neurotechnology, and Canada Research Chair in Translational Neuroscience and Dementia. Her research focuses on Alzheimer’s disease, the most common cause of dementia.
“A lot of sleep disruption could increase your risk of dementia,” says Kent.
“What we know is that there’s a protein called amyloid beta, which accumulates in the brain and causes these plaques in the brains of individuals who have dementia. Amyloid beta is this toxic protein, a waste product of your brain. These plaques accumulate for, on average, about 20 years before dementia starts.”
Sleep plays a role in how quickly that protein is removed, linking repeated sleep loss to a process that can unfold over decades.
She concludes, “During sleep, that protein is cleared out at a faster rate. So if you’re continuously missing sleep, then that protein and those plaques will accumulate at a faster rate. Not everyone who has poor sleep will get Alzheimer’s disease, but if you are somebody who has the predisposition for the disease, then missing sleep over time will drive the process.”
Reference: “Young and old adult brains experience opposite effects of acute sleep restriction on the functional connectivity network” by Josh Neudorf, Leanne Rokos, Kelly Shen, Brianne Kent and Anthony R. McIntosh, 18 June 2026,
Imaging Neuroscience
DOI: 10.1162/IMAG.a.1278

title: A Hidden Substance in Drinking Water May Be Linked to Heart Problems in Children
content:
A large study involving millions of children has uncovered a possible connection between naturally occurring lithium in drinking water and a rare heart rhythm disorder. The condition, known as Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, involves an abnormal electrical pathway in the heart that can trigger episodes of dangerously rapid heartbeats. Credit: Shutterstock
The water we drink may hold clues to a rare heart condition in children, but whether naturally occurring lithium plays a role in its development remains unknown.
A dangerously fast heartbeat can begin with an extra strand of heart muscle that forms before birth. The strand creates an abnormal electrical connection, allowing the heart’s rhythm to go awry. Doctors can eliminate these connections, but a larger question has remained largely unanswered. Why do they develop in the first place?
A study led by
UC San Francisco
researchers points to a possible environmental clue in drinking water. Children living in areas with higher levels of naturally occurring lithium were more likely to be diagnosed with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, or WPW, a rare condition involving a particular type of abnormal connection. The findings, published online in
The Journal of Clinical Investigation
, show an association, but do not establish that lithium causes the condition.
These connections, known as accessory pathways, usually occur in people with no family history of the condition. That suggests environmental exposures during fetal development could play a role. Lithium attracted the researchers’ attention because medicinal doses taken during pregnancy have been associated with an increased risk of congenital heart defects, including Ebstein’s anomaly. This rare defect is frequently accompanied by accessory pathways, prompting the team to investigate whether lithium in drinking water might also be associated with changes in the developing heart.
Higher lithium, greater odds of WPW
The researchers analyzed health and water-quality data for more than 2.3 million children in California. Just 686 had a documented WPW diagnosis. Children living in counties with lithium levels in the highest 25% had 71% greater odds of a diagnosis than those in counties with lower levels.
The team then tested its main finding among nearly 2 million children in New York. There, children living in areas with lithium levels above 10 parts per billion also had greater odds of a WPW diagnosis.
Higher lithium levels in California were also associated with palpitations, fainting, and supraventricular tachycardia, or SVT, a rapid heart rhythm that can cause palpitations and other symptoms. Accessory pathways are among the most common causes of SVT. WPW is also associated with a small increased risk of sudden death. Doctors can treat accessory pathways with catheter ablation, a minimally invasive procedure that eliminates the small area of heart tissue responsible for the abnormal electrical connection.
“We’ve known about these pathways for decades, and we know how to treat them, but we haven’t known why people develop them,” said Gregory Marcus, MD, MAS, an endowed professor in atrial fibrillation research in the UCSF Division of Cardiology and senior author of the study. “This is an exciting step because it points to a potential environmental factor that may be modifiable. But we need more research to determine whether lithium is actually contributing to their development.”
Individual lithium exposure remains unknown
The study estimated exposure from the county of residence. Researchers did not know how much lithium individual children or their mothers consumed, and other environmental or genetic factors could help explain the association. Studies in other populations and research that measures exposure during pregnancy more precisely are needed to determine whether lithium plays a causal role.
Marcus said the findings should not alarm people about the safety of their drinking water, including those who are pregnant. Despite the association, WPW was rare in the children studied.
Lithium occurs naturally in groundwater, and its concentration varies widely by location. Groundwater used for drinking water across the United States and elsewhere contains lithium, raising questions about the findings’ potential public health significance beyond California and New York. The researchers said the results underscore the value of collecting environmental data to understand how ordinary exposures may affect health.
“We’re exposed to things in our environment every day, including substances that occur naturally,” Marcus said. “The more precisely we can measure those exposures and connect them with health outcomes, the better we can understand what may be influencing health.”
Lithium in drinking water is not currently regulated in the United States, although the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency requires monitoring through its program for unregulated contaminants. The U.S. Geological Survey also measures lithium in groundwater.
“The next step is to determine whether lithium itself is contributing to the development of these pathways and, if so, how much exposure matters and when during development it matters most,” Marcus said. “That will require studies that can measure exposure much more precisely.”
Reference: “Elevated lithium levels in drinking water are associated with higher prevalence of Wolff-Parkinson-White diagnoses” by Justin T. Teraoka, Anushree Agarwal, Janet J. Tang, Thomas A. Dewland and Gregory M. Marcus, 13 October 2026,
The Journal of Clinical Investigation
DOI: 10.1172/JCI205020

title: Scientists Find a Clever Way to Read Quantum Information Without Destroying It
content:
Schematic of a readout of an Andreev qubit without using auxiliary qubits. Credit: Marcus Egues and José Carlos Egues, with assistance from ChatGPT
Simulations suggest that one type of qubit could reveal its state through its own electric current, helping researchers monitor quantum computers with less disturbance and fewer components.
Like a bit in an ordinary computer, a qubit stores information using states labeled 0 and 1. A qubit can also be prepared in a superposition, a quantum combination of the two. These states belong to a physical system that researchers build and control. In the design explored here, that system is a tiny wire connected to superconducting materials.
The aim of quantum computing is to use quantum behavior to perform certain calculations more efficiently than conventional computers. That requires control: researchers must prepare qubits and change their states deliberately. Unwanted interactions with the surroundings can disrupt them, and measuring a qubit can alter it, too.
A theoretical study proposes reading one type of qubit through an electric current it produces itself. This could let researchers follow its behavior with minimal disturbance and without the extra qubits used in many existing methods.
Quantum information in a tiny wire
Andreev qubits hold information in states formed between superconducting materials, which carry electric current without resistance. They are named after Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939–2023), who described the underlying process at the boundary between normal and superconducting materials in 1964.
“In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot—that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined – formed in an indium arsenide [
] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It’s in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed,” explains José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil.
Schematic of a readout of an Andreev qubit without using auxiliary qubits. In the proposed device, the qubit’s quantum information appears as an oscillating supercurrent circulating in a large superconducting loop. The magnetic signal generated by this current is detected by a small coil coupled to a SQUID, allowing the qubit’s state to be inferred with minimal perturbation. Credit: Marcus Egues and José Carlos Egues, with assistance from ChatGPT
“In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained,” says Egues.
Many existing methods use a helper quantum system called an ancilla. Researchers prepare it, connect it to the qubit, transfer information to it, and measure it to preserve the original qubit as much as possible. These steps add time and equipment. “Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself,” says Egues.
Reading the signal a qubit produces
The qubit would sit in a closed superconducting circuit carrying a supercurrent, an electric current that flows without resistance. The calculations predict that interference between the states in the qubit’s superposition makes part of this current oscillate. “It’s precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It’s that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal,” Egues points out.
An applied voltage usually causes this kind of oscillation, known as the AC Josephson effect. “Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It’s the very evolution of the qubit’s state that produces that oscillation,” says Egues.
A nearby superconducting quantum interference device, or SQUID, would act as the detector. These instruments are extremely sensitive to weak magnetic fields. Egues explains, “We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID ‘senses’ that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.”
Identifying the qubit’s state requires knowing both the balance of 0 and 1 and their relative phase, or how the two components line up.
“Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it’s possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit,” Egues explains.
Researchers could also track the qubit through repeated readings without resetting it to its initial state after each measurement.
The design still needs experimental testing
Simulations included measurement noise and feedback from the small detection coil. They indicated that the detector’s influence could become negligible, with readout accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%, depending on the number of measurements. These values fall within standard thresholds adopted in quantum error correction schemes.
“Our method doesn’t eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits – the ancillas – employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols,” Egues notes.
The work, published in
Physical Review B Letters
, was led by Egues and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. SQUID detection of extremely small currents and magnetic fields is already established, and Egues says the proposal would not require future advances in materials or device fabrication.
“All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn’t yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed,” he argues.
Reference: “Andreev qubit readout from dynamic interference supercurrent” by Xian-Peng Zhang, Chuanchang Zeng, Zhen-Biao Yang, Jose Carlos Egues and Yugui Yao, 5 August 2026,
Physical Review B

title: Chemical Breakthrough Could Unlock the “Holy Grail” of Solid-State Battery Technology
content:
Technology
Solid-state batteries are a promising alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries because they replace flammable liquid electrolytes with solid materials. Credit: Stock
A simple chemical treatment could overcome a persistent weakness in next-generation solid-state batteries.
Scientists in China have developed a thin protective coating that could help overcome a major obstacle to longer-lasting, high-capacity batteries. In laboratory tests, solid-state batteries using the treated lithium metal retained 82.3% of their initial capacity after 300 charging cycles, compared with just 43.0% for batteries using untreated lithium.
The researchers at Xidian University developed a simple liquid coating that reacts with lithium metal to form a protective barrier. Their findings, published in
Science China Chemistry
, suggest a possible route toward safer, more durable batteries for electric vehicles and energy storage.
Solving a Persistent Battery Problem
Lithium metal has been called the “holy grail” of energy storage because it can theoretically store nearly ten times as much charge per gram as the graphite used in conventional lithium-ion batteries. Its exceptional capacity could enable lighter batteries that store more energy and potentially support longer driving ranges.
To address this problem, researchers led by Professors Siwu Li, Weiwei Wu, and Chuang Yu combined a silicon-based polymer with indium chloride. When applied to lithium, the mixture forms lithium fluoride and lithium-indium alloy nanoparticles within a flexible protective film just 12 micrometers thick (about 0.00047 inches).
“This hybrid layer acts like a smart fortress,” explains corresponding author Siwu Li. “The polymer backbone provides flexibility to absorb the mechanical stress of lithium expanding and contracting. The lithium fluoride phase blocks electrons to prevent dendrite nucleation. And the lithium-indium alloy nanoparticles act as traffic conductors, guiding lithium ions to deposit evenly rather than piling up in dangerous spikes.”
This illustration depicts the in-situ formation of the PFSIn-Li interlayer on a lithium metal anode. A liquid precursor containing a fluorinated siloxane polymer and indium salt reacts on the lithium surface to generate a multifunctional hybrid film. The organic polymer network interpenetrates with inorganic lithium fluoride, lithium-indium alloy, and lithium silicon oxide nanodomains, simultaneously suppressing dendrite growth and stabilizing the interface with the sulfide solid electrolyte. Credit: Science China Press
Stronger Performance in Laboratory Tests
The coated lithium electrodes withstood a critical current density of 3.5 milliamperes per square centimeter, more than four times the 0.8 achieved by untreated lithium. In complete batteries containing a nickel-cobalt-manganese oxide cathode and a sulfide solid electrolyte, the protected electrodes delivered an initial capacity of 129.8 milliampere-hours per gram and retained 82.3% after 300 cycles at 0.5C.
Spectroscopy and electron microscopy confirmed the coating’s composition and revealed a dense, uniform layer without visible cracks or gaps.
A Simpler Path to Better Batteries
The coating could help address the chemical instability between lithium metal and sulfide solid electrolytes, a major challenge in solid-state battery development.
Because the protective layer forms from an applied liquid, it may be compatible with existing industrial coating equipment without requiring expensive vacuum processing. The researchers also plan to explore alternatives to indium, including tin and zinc.
Although commercial performance remains unproven, the findings offer a promising approach to making high-energy lithium metal batteries more stable and longer-lasting.

title: Kids Who Learn To Swim Early May Have an Unexpected Advantage in School
content:
Early swimming lessons may offer unexpected advantages in childhood development. Credit: Shutterstock
Children who learn to swim early may have a head start in classroom skills, with research finding developmental advantages even after accounting for socioeconomic background.
When family budgets tighten, swimming lessons can be among the first expenses to go. Most swim schools operate as commercial businesses, and cost is the biggest barrier to participation. Yet the consequences of missing out may extend beyond water safety and fitness to the skills children need when they start school.
A four-year study involving nearly 7,000 survey respondents and individual testing of 177 children suggests that children who learn to swim early have developmental advantages over their peers. Participants younger than 5 could be 5 to 18 months ahead of typical milestones in literacy, numeracy, and following instructions compared with the general population of children their age. Those advantages remained when socioeconomic background was taken into account.
Robyn Jorgensen, Emeritus Professor at the University of Canberra in Australia, examines and expands on the research in her new book,
Why Young Children Should Learn to Swim
Swimming may offer a classroom head start
Jorgensen does not interpret the findings as evidence that children who learn to swim are innately smarter. Instead, she argues that lessons develop skills and habits children can carry into the classroom. A child counting kicks from one to ten with an instructor, for example, is practicing number sequencing and one-to-one correspondence, matching each number to a single action.
The project grew out of a conversation between Jorgensen and Laurie Lawrence, an Olympic swim coach inducted into both the Australian and U.S. Swimming Halls of Fame. Lawrence thought children who learned to swim early generally seemed more “school-ready.”
“There was no formal evidence to support this observation, but it was one that Laurie felt he and many others in the swim industry observed,” Jorgensen explains.
To investigate that “industry hunch,” Jorgensen and her colleagues used the Peabody Developmental Motor Scales and Woodcock-Johnson III assessments. These internationally recognized testing tools were normed against national census data, providing reference standards for comparing the children’s performance with that of the wider population.
The results surprised even Jorgensen, who said, “My early observations of the young learners piqued my interest while retaining some sense of skepticism about what could be achieved. I am not from a swimming background, so had no vested interest in the ‘proving’ or otherwise of Laurie’s hunch. My only interest in swimming was as a grandparent and around water safety for my children and grandchildren, and as a recreational activity.”
Beyond the literacy and numeracy findings, the research suggests that early swimming participants are more sociable and have measurable advantages in cognitive development, language skills, and emotional regulation. These findings point to potential benefits for academic success.
“It is reasonable to claim that swimming prepares children for the schooling years, particularly the early years and the transition into schooling,” Jorgensen explains.
Costly lessons and faraway pools
Access to those potential benefits is sharply unequal. Jorgensen’s analysis identifies the United States and China as having the greatest inequities in access, with regular swimming lessons affordable only to very affluent families. Singapore, Australia, Brazil, and South Africa also face substantial economic and geographic barriers.
One respondent from Zimbabwe described how lessons compete with basic necessities. “So swimming is still seen in Africa in general as elite. But basically, if you are a working-level person well below average, swimming lessons will not be a priority; what will be a priority is feeding your family.”
Even reaching a pool can be difficult. In Australia, families on remote farming properties can face journeys of hundreds of kilometers to the nearest one. The study describes “a double whammy” for children from low-income and rural communities, who are both the least likely to have access to lessons and the most at risk of drowning.
The case for subsidizing swimming lessons
With cost-of-living pressures affecting families worldwide, Jorgensen is calling for broader government support. She argues that governments have both a moral and a financial incentive to intervene, given the billions they already spend trying to close gaps in school achievement.
“What this study has shown is that even when socioeconomic backgrounds are accounted for, children who participate in quality lessons achieve better than the general population. It would make sense for the government to consider investing in providing or subsidizing early years swimming for families who would otherwise be excluded from participation in early years swimming lessons,” Jorgensen explains.
“Investing in quality swimming lessons would make a politically wise move. The cost of lessons can be quite high, but if policies were created to offer subsidies for parents or to create swim programs for disadvantaged families, there is considerable potential for adding capital to these cohorts of learners,” she explains.

title: Could Type 2 Diabetes Be Reversed? 14-Year Study Reveals Remarkable Results
content:
Weight-loss surgery may offer more than significant weight reduction for people with type 2 diabetes. Research suggests it can improve blood sugar control and even lead to remission. Credit: Shutterstock
In a long-term trial, weight-loss surgery led to more type 2 diabetes remissions than intensive medical and lifestyle management, while patients’ disease histories offered clues to who might benefit most.
For some people with type 2 diabetes, keeping blood sugar under control without medication is possible. This state, known as remission, raises a question that could shape years of treatment decisions: Which approaches give people the best chance of reaching it, and what makes it more likely to last?
A long-term study found that 58% of participants assigned to weight-loss surgery achieved remission during follow-up, compared with 3% of those assigned to intensive medical and lifestyle management. Participants were followed for a median of 11 years, with some followed for up to 14 years. Those percentages describe how many people reached remission, rather than how many remained in remission throughout that time.
Researchers analyzed data from 262 people with type 2 diabetes, including 166 assigned to metabolic-bariatric surgery, commonly called weight-loss surgery, and 96 assigned to medical and lifestyle management. They defined remission as an A1C below 6.5% without blood sugar-lowering medication. A1C is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.
The findings were published in
Diabetes Care
, a journal of the American Diabetes Association®. They come from the Alliance of Randomized Trials of Medicine vs. Metabolic Surgery in Type 2 Diabetes (ARMMS-T2D), the largest, longest-running trial of metabolic surgery for diabetes. The study’s lead author is Donald Simonson, M.D., MPH, Sc.D., of Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School in Boston.
Diabetes history offers clues to lasting remission
Participants who had lived with diabetes for fewer years, did not use insulin, and took fewer types of blood sugar-lowering medications before treatment were more likely to achieve remission. Greater weight loss during the first year after treatment was also associated with a higher likelihood of remission.
John P. Kirwan, Ph.D., is the principal investigator of a recently published clinical trial showing that people with type 2 diabetes were much more likely to achieve remission after weight-loss surgery than after intensive medical and lifestyle management. Kirwan is executive director of the University of Oklahoma Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center. Credit: University of Oklahoma
Among people who initially reached remission, diabetes was more likely to return in those who had lived with the disease longer and those who took more types of blood sugar-lowering medications before treatment. Together, these associations suggest that a patient’s diabetes history and response to treatment may help physicians assess both the likelihood of remission and its potential duration.
A case for considering surgery earlier
The study’s principal investigator, John P. Kirwan, Ph.D., was named executive director of the University of Oklahoma Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center this summer. He also serves as Vice Provost for Diabetes Programs at the University of Oklahoma and holds the Chickasaw Nation Endowed Chair in Diabetes Research.
“For years, one of the most consequential questions in diabetes care has been whether the benefits of metabolic surgery endure,” Kirwan said. “Now we have a durable answer. Over 14 years, 58% of surgical patients achieved remission, compared with just 3% on medication and lifestyle alone. By identifying who is most likely to achieve lasting remission, including shorter diabetes duration, no insulin use, and greater early weight loss, we can offer surgery to the right people earlier, rather than as a last resort.”
Kirwan has led the study since its inception, through his years at the Cleveland Clinic and the Pennington Biomedical Research Center at Louisiana State University. He now brings his expertise in translational and clinical research to the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus.
“Recruiting Dr. Kirwan to lead the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center brings to Oklahoma one of the world’s foremost authorities on long-term treatment for type 2 diabetes,” said Gary Raskob, Ph.D., Senior Vice President and Provost of the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. “Research of this caliber is exactly what this center, and Harold Hamm’s investment in it, was created to advance.”
Reference: “Predictors of Type 2 Diabetes Remission and Relapse After Metabolic-Bariatric Surgery or Medical-Lifestyle Therapy in the ARMMS-T2D Study” by Donald C. Simonson, David E. Cummings, Philip R. Schauer, Ali Aminian, Bo Hu, David E. Arterburn, John M. Jakicic, Sangeeta R. Kashyap, Ashley H. Vernon, William F. Gourash, Anita P. Courcoulas, Mary Elizabeth Patti and John P. Kirwan, 20 October 2026,

title: The Secret to Saving Shellfish From Acidifying Oceans Could Be Hiding in Crushed Shells
content:
In the study, UC Davis researchers added crushed shells, pictured here, to sand to better understand how the practice can protect shell-making animals from the negative effects of ocean acidification. Credit: Hannah Kempf/UC Davis
Crushed shells helped young clams grow larger shells in laboratory tests, showing how a long-standing Indigenous coastal practice can offer local protection against ocean acidification.
For a young clam, the surrounding water can threaten the shell it is trying to grow. When seawater absorbs excess carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, it becomes more acidic, making shell growth more difficult and energetically costly for animals such as clams, oysters, and mussels. Acidic seawater can even dissolve shells. Larvae and juveniles are thought to be especially vulnerable to this process, known as ocean acidification.
Indigenous communities have long added crushed shells to coastal sands to help keep these ecosystems healthy. Research from the
University of California, Davis
now helps explain how this material, called shell hash, can protect young clams from some of acidification’s effects. Published in
Biogeosciences
, the study connects the chemistry of water between sand grains with changes in clam growth and gene activity.
Raising groups of Pacific littleneck clams in four different conditions, the researchers monitored their growth and the water’s chemistry over a 90-day period. Credit: Hannah Kempf/UC Davis
Crushed shells help young clams grow
At the UC Davis Bodega Marine Laboratory, researchers raised baby Pacific littleneck clams in four conditions. Two groups burrowed in sediment beneath either non-acidified or acidified seawater. The other two experienced the same seawater conditions, but their sediment contained shell hash. During the 90-day experiment, the team tracked shell growth and sampled the seawater three times a week, monitoring acidity, salinity, temperature, and dissolved oxygen.
“We found that, on average, clams grew larger shells when shell hash was present in their treatment,” said study first author Hannah Kempf, an environmental scientist at the California State Water Board who graduated from UC Davis with a Ph.D. in earth and planetary sciences in 2024. “Interestingly, we also found that, on a genetic level, the ‘acidification’ signal was dramatically minimized when shell hash was present.”
The crushed shells altered the chemistry of the water filling the tiny spaces between sand particles, reducing its overall acidity and creating better conditions for shell growth. That finding places the protection at a very local scale, in the water surrounding the burrowing clams.
A weaker acidification signal in clam genes
“Adding crushed shells removed the negative genetic changes that occur when young clams are raised in acidified water,” said study corresponding author David Gold, an associate professor of earth and planetary sciences at UC Davis.
A UC Davis researcher holds a Pacific littleneck clam. Credit: Hannah Kempf/UC Davis
To examine gene activity, the researchers collected samples of the clams’ mantle tissue, which produces their shells, after 90 days and used them for follow-up gene sequencing. The analysis revealed gene expression profiles, or patterns of activity across genes. In clams raised in acidified seawater with shell hash, those profiles were largely indistinguishable from those of clams raised in non-acidified water.
“This was the first time the question was studied from a genetic perspective,” Gold said.
Indigenous expertise could shape coastal research
Traditional ecological knowledge provides significant evidence that shell hash benefits shell-making animals, said study co-author Tsim Schneider, an associate professor of anthropology at UC Santa Cruz. In the Pacific Northwest, some Indigenous communities build large-scale structures that expand intertidal spaces, the areas of shore between high and low tide. These structures promote habitat for invertebrates and other marine organisms.
“For me, one of the interesting aspects of this research is the potential to engage more fully with tribes on designing projects that promote their long-standing expertise and Indigenous science,” said Schneider, who is also affiliated with the National Science Foundation’s Center for Braiding Indigenous Knowledges and Science. “If there’s a history of adding shell hash to clam beds in California, for example, western science might be able to better support communities interested in reawakening dormant cultural knowledge and coastal stewardship practices.”
Reference: “Shell hash promotes growth in Pacific littleneck clams (
Leukoma staminea
) by altering pore water chemistry” by Hannah L. Kempf, Alyssa J. Griffin, Gabriel Ng, Tessa M. Hill, Tsim D. Schneider, Sandra J. Carlson and David A. Gold, 29 October 2026,
Biogeosciences
DOI: 10.5194/bg-23-7627-2026
The research was supported by a California Sea Grant and the Russell J. and Dorothy S. Bilinski Fellowship.

title: Perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell reaches efficiency of 35.1% with 85% fill factor
content:
Perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell reaches efficiency of 35.1% with 85% fill factor
Researchers from Soochow University, Northwestern Polytechnical University, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University,
, the CNPC Tubular Goods Research Institute, KAUST, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Xi’an Jiaotong University and Suzhou Laboratory have developed a molecular design for the hole-selective layer of perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells, and report a certified stabilized efficiency of 35.1%.
In tandem cells built on textured silicon, self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) face a trade-off, according to the researchers: more conjugated molecules conduct better, but they tend to aggregate, which impairs conformal coverage of the rough, pyramid-textured surface. The team addressed this with molecules that have a tailored intramolecular distortion, which suppresses excess π–π stacking without sacrificing charge transport.
The researchers say this produces a highly ordered, conformal SAM across the pyramidal textures. The interface also provides energy-level alignment for fast charge extraction, improves defect passivation through adaptive conformational adjustment of the molecules, and acts as a template for growing high-quality perovskite films.
Using this interface, the tandem device reached a fill factor of 85% and a certified stabilized power conversion efficiency of 35.1%. In aging tests under the ISOS-L-1 protocol, it retained more than 94% of its initial performance after 1,500 hours.

title: New synchrotron platform enables researchers to watch perovskite solar cells at work on the nanoscale
content:
New synchrotron platform enables researchers to watch perovskite solar cells at work on the nanoscale
Researchers at the Brazilian Center for Research in Energy and Materials (CNPEM), led by Rodrigo Szostak and Hélio C. N. Tolentino of its Brazilian Synchrotron Light Laboratory (LNLS), have developed a sample holder that allows complete solar cells to be studied with X-ray nanoscopy while they operate. The platform was installed at the Tarumã station of the Carnaúba nanoprobe beamline at the Sirius synchrotron in Campinas, and it was designed mainly for perovskite solar cells.
The holder controls temperature, atmosphere, illumination and electrical bias while X-ray fluorescence, diffraction and absorption spectroscopy map the cell’s chemistry and structure at a scale of about 200 nm. The authors say that nanoscale operando characterization of perovskites with focused X-rays had not been achieved before; earlier operando studies were done on bulk samples.
The cell is built on an ITO-coated glass chip, with platinum circuits on the back acting as a heater and a temperature sensor. Heating is confined to a 3 × 3 mm area, to limit thermal drift. Infrared imaging showed a temperature variation of 0.85 °C across the area at 150 °C, and the chip reaches its target temperature in under two minutes. A titanium alloy mount with flexible elements lets the glass expand without cracking, and a sealed chamber allows gases to flow while humidity is monitored at the inlet and outlet. Illumination comes from a broadband white LED, chosen because its spectrum is closest to sunlight among the LEDs the team evaluated.
When cycled between 30 and 150 °C over about 20 hours, the sample moved about 5 µm vertically and about 1 µm horizontally, reproducibly and reversibly. “We have excellent positional stability,” Szostak said, adding that to his knowledge the holder likely offers the best positional stability achieved for this type of experiment.
The team demonstrated the platform on a complete n-i-p perovskite cell. They recorded current-voltage curves and the response to switching the light on and off, mapped iodine and lead with X-ray fluorescence, and imaged perovskite grains of about 2 µm with diffraction. The lattice parameter increased as the temperature rose from 40 °C to 65 °C, as expected.
The platform still has limits. Illumination reaches one sun only when the LED sits directly in front of the cell, which blocks some X-ray geometries. In the lateral configuration used at the beamline, the cell receives about 30% of one sun, and improving that is a next step. The ITO chip works up to 150 °C, or up to 300 °C for experiments that don’t need a conductive substrate.
The holder is now a multi-user facility. It can also be used for organic, quantum-dot and dye-sensitized cells and for LEDs.

title: Swift Solar begins shipping HJT cells to US space customers, plans to fly perovskite-silicon tandems
content:
Swift Solar begins shipping HJT cells to US space customers, plans to fly perovskite-silicon tandems
Swift Solar
says it has started shipping silicon heterojunction (HJT) solar cells to US space customers, while continuing to test perovskite cells in orbit and working toward perovskite-silicon tandems for space.
The company positions HJT as an alternative to the PERC cells used in many existing satellite systems. It cites an initial efficiency of about 25%, compared with about 23% for PERC under AM1.5 conditions, and a temperature coefficient of -0.25%/°C, compared with -0.35%/°C. Swift estimates this gives around 10% more power at beginning of life, and says thinner HJT cells also retain more power at end of life and reduce weight. The HJT cells follow Swift’s acquisition of Meyer Burger’s manufacturing assets and IP in March.
On the perovskite side, Swift says it began flying its cells in 2023 and has completed three low Earth orbit test missions. In the longest mission, single-junction perovskite cells showed no meaningful efficiency loss over seven months, which the company says is equivalent to more than 3,000 sunrises. Swift adds that this does not yet establish performance over a full LEO mission lifetime or readiness for mission-critical systems.
The next step, according to the company, is to fly full-size perovskite-silicon tandem cells. Swift says tandems built by adding a perovskite layer on HJT cells can deliver more than 20% more power than HJT alone. It also says its work on perovskites for space includes published research on radiation tolerance, self-healing and high-temperature operation.
